Judge a presentation by whether the audience understood, believed, and remembered the content, not by whether the speaker's style matched a prescribed model; humble and charismatic deliveries both succeed, but stylistic diversity does not make every style acceptable.

Check a talk against three traits rather than one: content worth the audience's time, visible passion for it, and a keen sense of who the audience is, what they already know, why they are listening, and what preconceptions they hold — strong content can carry an unconventional delivery, but no delivery rescues a talk aimed at the wrong audience.

Show genuine enthusiasm in the speaker's own register rather than imitating another presenter's exuberance; a manufactured display reads as disingenuous, and against an audience that disbelieves the idea even charismatic speakers soften to a quiet but earnest delivery.

Accept that no single delivery style is correct — a poised professional manner and an unpolished but passionate one both hold audiences, and a speaker who violates every prescribed rule of dress, eye contact, and stance can still distinguish themselves through sincere passion, deep knowledge, and sensitivity to the audience — so develop a style from what the speaker is actually comfortable giving.

Account for the audience and the room when judging a delivery: a familiar smiling audience invites movement, storytelling, humour, and vocal variation while an unfamiliar or hostile one naturally produces a more businesslike manner, and a large tiered hall imposes a formal barrier that approaching the front rows only partly bridges — so criticising a speaker's warmth without accounting for the audience they faced is unfair.
Judge a presentation by whether the audience was transformed — able to understand something new or do something differently — since audience transformation is the goal of persuasion.

Judge a presentation by whether the audience looks enlightened, moved to act, or willing to change behaviour, and get there by reviewing the content through their eyes, showing them something they have never seen, and combining strong stories with convincing information delivered humanly.
Cut unnecessary detail until the main takeaways survive: burying key findings among extraneous details or on busy decorated slides is the most common way a technically sound talk fails.
Do not apply the preview-tell-summarize structure to an audience strongly biased against the results; announcing the conclusion up front to opponents costs the speaker the hearing.
Give projected slides disproportionate attention in review, because they shape not only what the audience comprehends but how the speaker prepares and delivers.
Pitch the slides at the depth the speech can actually deliver, because slides flashed past for seconds leave the audience with unanswered questions while the speech stays shallow.

Strip every phrase and decorative image that does not connect directly to the spoken content, since audiences understand and remember more when extraneous information is removed; the working target is the slide's signal-to-noise ratio.

Do not put on a slide everything the speaker will say, because when all of it is already written many listeners tune the speaker out and read instead — whereas speaking the supporting details from images demonstrates ownership and raises credibility.

Include title, outline, and conclusion slides only where they earn their place, since they carry organisation rather than content and the shorter the talk the less each is needed; a research-conference talk needs no outline slide, and opening on a blank black slide with the focus on the speaker can be effective when the audience already holds a concrete image of the topic.

Identify the message for every scene before the talk whether or not it will appear on the slide, since that act itself focuses the presentation; where the message is left off, the whole burden of communicating it falls on the speaker, who must settle the assertion beforehand and practise enough to state and support it while looking at the audience.

Stop tinkering with slides in time to rehearse, since effort spent far beyond the communication requirement at the cost of rehearsal produces a talk in which the speaker can find neither a rhythm nor the transitions between scenes.

Diagnose an underperforming scientific talk against three errors first: a scope too broad to reach a satisfying depth, slides that bury the main message in the noise of bulleted lists, and delivery without the passion or confidence the message deserves.
Diagnose a failing presentation at the structural level first, because most presentations that fail do so from structural deficiencies and when the structure is sound the presentation is sound.

Use the persuasive power of presentations to build up rather than deceive: presentations carried criminal counts in the Enron prosecutions, a slick pitch pushed a fraud past an audience that sensed it was too good to be true, and communication that abandons reason and truth becomes propaganda that obliterates the credibility of everyone involved when it collapses.

Diagnose a failing slide at the level of construction rather than style, because in the vast majority of cases the fundamentals are what failed and the mechanics of a well-built slide are the presenter's most important tool.

Always issue a handout when the slide information is complex or dense, preferably at the end so paper does not rustle during the talk, and include an appendix of the dense data so the audience can verify the facts.
Build slides that convey technical information from a succinct sentence assertion supported by visual evidence, not from a phrase headline over a bulleted subtopic list.
Recognise the topic-subtopic structure — a phrase headline naming the topic over bullets naming subordinate ideas — as the dominant pattern in scientific slides and as the thing to be replaced.

Put relevant visual evidence — a photograph, drawing, diagram, graph, or film — on every projected slide, because images are processed by a different channel from text and people learn more effectively from words plus relevant pictures than from words alone.

Audit a deck against the five measured failures of scientific slides: phrase headlines, bulleted lists, missing relevant images, stock decorative backgrounds, and a reading load of 35 or more words a minute.

Apply the assertion-evidence structure as a pair of substitutions: a succinct sentence stating the slide's main assertion — a hypothesis, assumption, insight, or result — in place of the phrase headline, and visual evidence in place of the bulleted list, with bulleted lists not occurring at all.

Attribute the assertion-evidence advantage to emphasis: the most important details are carried by the sentence headline or the visual evidence, whereas in a topic-subtopic slide the audience cannot separate primary from secondary details in the bullets and the visual evidence must share space with the list.

Expect the structure's largest effect on preparation rather than delivery: the sentence-assertion headline forces the speaker to identify each slide's most important takeaway and only then select the evidence for it, converging on more effective evidence where a phrase headline commonly does the opposite.

Keep the balance between what is shown and what is said: the headline carries the main message, the body carries the evidence, and the secondary details such as how the experiment was run are supplied aloud — which both builds credibility by demonstrating ownership and lets the same slide sequence flex to the audience and the time available.

Expect crafting the sentence-assertion headline to be the hardest part of the work, since it demands identifying each slide's single most important message rather than naming a topic; read in sequence, those headlines should give the bare-bones story of the work for the speaker to flesh out aloud.

Sequence the slides so the opening assertion is an entry point that motivates the audience and arouses curiosity, the key insights from what is already known come next, and the experimental result that tested them comes last.

Let the visual evidence alone trigger what to say, which requires practising with the slides and which is what produces the natural delivery; with such slides there are only two legitimate reasons to look at the screen — a glance to confirm the slide advanced, and pointing out a detail the audience is already looking at.

Choose the type of visual evidence from the assertion it must support — a map and photographs for a background fact, photographs with a timeline and graph for a trend, a diagram for a process, a line or bar graph for a quantitative relationship — because well-chosen visual evidence lets the audience grasp the connections at a glance where a bulleted list cannot.

Treat the 28-point assertion headline as an established standard rather than a novelty, since it has been the norm for assertion headlines at a national laboratory for more than three decades and is endorsed by other slide designers.

Use assertion-evidence for the large majority of scientific slides while recognising that special audiences, purposes, or occasions call for other equally grounded structures — chiefly the TED style for the general public — with four sequencing variations available: evidence-assertion order, pecha kucha, Lessig, and Prezi.

Never project an assertion with no visual evidence at all, even though showing evidence before the assertion is legitimate: some image must be present to exploit the audience's ability to process a picture while listening, and on a white background a headline-only slide leaves over 80 percent of the screen glaring back at them.

Settle the story before opening the slide software: write the main message and each supporting assertion on separate sticky notes, arrange them into the order that tells the best story, and treat that as the argument — the steps that carry the audience to the main message — after which any detail supporting none of them is excluded.

Replace the phrase-headline-plus-bulleted-list default with the assertion-evidence structure, accepting the greater creation time when the message is important, because the comprehension gain grows with the technical difficulty of the content.
Check slide headlines on whether each slide conveys a message and serves the audience, whether each headline states the key assertion, and whether each is succinct at one or two lines.

Check visual evidence on whether it supports the assertion and was explained, the level of detail is appropriate with extraneous details excluded, bullet lists were avoided and text blocks held to one or two lines, reference listings of author and year were given, and fewer than 20 words per minute were projected.

Follow the build sequence in order — collect and create, filter to the big idea, cluster by topic, charge topics into sentences, order for impact, attach supporting slides, confirm the turning points, validate all three contrasts — and only then turn words into pictures, because structure is what lets an audience follow the presenter's thought process.

Split content across slides and reveal the pieces in sequence whenever secondary or technical detail competes with the slide's single main message, keeping on the slide only what is addressed verbally; splitting without sequencing does not by itself solve density.

Compose every data chart in three layers — neutral background context, the data at enough contrast to read at a distance, and a foreground emphasis layer carrying the key conclusion — because the slide's job is conclusions and insight while handouts carry the dense data.

Refuse slide rules that have no research basis — such as the 6-by-6 rule — and treat all presentation rules as carrying exceptions, grounding advice in the observed traits of excellent presenters instead.
Put the presenter's name and organisational identity on the title slide, since omitting them forfeits an easy chance to establish authority.

Consider abandoning projected slides entirely when the primary purpose is to inspire; a theatrical opener can far outperform a conventional slide talk, but only when the persona and material genuinely fit the audience and only once, since its power comes from the audience not knowing what will happen.
Make the slides carry the main assertions and their evidence when presenting remotely, because the speaker can neither read expressions nor adjust to them.
Accept that a bad presentation can be worse than no presentation, since the same hour spent in direct discussion among the attendees may communicate more.
Lower dependency on slides, because overuse diminishes human connection and an audience judges a presentation successful when they feel they interacted with the presenter.

Solicit feedback nondefensively, let screeners challenge every assumption, and refuse the "yeah, but" or "if they really knew" excuses, because the presenter's receptivity to feedback determines the material's receptivity for everyone else.

Locate the usual failure upstream of slide design — the speaker has no compelling story before opening the software — and note that most presenters never even consider, let alone construct, where they intend to take the audience.

Rehearse being able to present without slides at all — imagining a power outage — because rejecting software-formed habits forces ownership of the content, and for a small audience non-projected aids such as flip charts, props, handouts, and physical devices increase the presenter's humanness.

Refuse to treat slides as an extension of the presenter's persona: the top concern is how well the message communicates, not how impressive the deck looks, since polish neither guarantees meaning nor substitutes for a missing strategy — and stage fear, ranking above the fear of dying, is not answered by prettier slides.
Treat presenting as a learnable skill worth deliberate investment, since presenters whose early talks were weak became strong ones later in their careers.

Hold judgments about a presenter's ability loosely: no one presents excellently every day, some are strong with colleagues yet stiff with strangers, and informed opinions about the same speaker vary widely.

Recognise that the weak common practice persists through inertia — easy defaults, saturation of the examples people see, and compelling institutional templates — and that this is exactly why rising above it distinguishes a presenter, with students and professionals who did so winning proposal competitions, jobs, and best-presentation awards.
Weigh the career cost of avoiding presentation, since the collaborator who presents receives the recognition and reticent partners have been overlooked for work they largely did.
Audience research pays off even when most of it never appears in the delivered talk, because the research is what produces the presenter's empathy and felt connection.

Sustaining a presentation that lives mostly in what could be requires a tightly rehearsed demonstration showing the new capability in humorous and unexpected ways; few presenters hold momentum there otherwise.

Invest in both the deck and the presenter's own visual-communication skill in proportion to the stakes, because presentations influence revenue, promotions, and behaviour change while bad slides are easy to make and costly.
Approach presentation development like a screenwriter rather than a speechwriter, being fluent in what the audience sees on screen, since the same material can be either documented or dramatized.

Choose the medium before designing the talk: ask whether a document or web page would deliver the information better, weighing that a presentation is expensive in aggregate hours but carries results far fresher than any publication cycle.

Weigh a presentation against a document on five advantages — fielding questions, reading expressions, delivery emphasis, richer visual aids, and evidenced receipt — against five disadvantages: one pass only, no time to look things up, the audience held to the speaker's pace, success hostage to delivery, and the difficulty of assembling everyone.
Budget the talk against a roughly twenty-minute attention span, and do not expect a presentation alone to carry a complex, deep technical subject.

Start preparation by specifying the assertions, insights, and results the audience should take away and only then match each to the available evidence; this costs more time than listing topics and subtopics but yields a more persuasive and more focused talk.

Allocate talk time by the significance of results rather than by the effort each activity consumed, since research presentations are judged on the quality of new insights communicated, not the quantity of work performed — which means excluding many tasks actually done.

Decide how much preparation a presentation deserves by asking how badly the idea needs to live, and then protect that time deliberately, because ordinary schedule pressure otherwise crowds out the planning a high-stakes talk requires.
Shift the effort from what the information is to how it is best communicated, because molding the information into an effective form is what separates an adequate presentation from a great one.
Expect the person who speaks about a result to receive the public credit for it, even when they acknowledge their collaborators, and let that shape who presents.

Treat specialists, managers, and policymakers as three distinct audiences whose failure to understand the work has three distinct costs: no one builds on it, institutions decide badly about it, and legislation on scientifically grounded problems proceeds without it.

Allot time for questions deliberately and choose their placement by format — a short talk is usually better served by holding them to the end, a longer or more interactive one by taking them throughout.

Watch the audience for cues of agreement, confusion, boredom, or disagreement throughout the talk and stay flexible enough to act on them, including improvising a concrete on-the-spot demonstration when a term the work depends on has visibly failed to land.

Exploit the channels only a live presentation has — pausing, changing volume, gesturing, moving closer, and visual aids a printed page cannot carry such as moving sequences, cheap colour, and physical demonstrations — rather than delivering a document aloud.

Use the TED style — few words if any, with powerful images that often fill the screen — when communicating science to the general public, designing it away from the computer by writing each takeaway on its own sticky note, ordering the notes, and building a slide only where a message warrants a scene.
Treat presentations as a glance medium closer to a billboard than to print: a slide's message must be graspable in about three seconds so attention can return to the presenter.

Draw or write while speaking when the audience must not read ahead: live marks keep them captive, a few key words or a sketch become a mnemonic they recall later, repeating the same sketch across sessions reinforces it, and a video feed lets the method scale to thousands.
Prefer a presentation with an attendance record when it matters legally or for compliance that the audience received the information, since a document may lie unopened.
Share only the right information for that exact moment and that specific audience, because presentations fail from too much information rather than too little.

Design every part of a talk for a single listening pass: a dropped negation misleads, and a listener who pauses to think about one idea loses everything said meanwhile, so load-bearing points must be redundant and recoverable.

Define every unfamiliar technical term and abbreviation the moment it is used, because an undefined term strands the audience and the damage compounds when the format defers questions to the end — while checking that the abbreviation is not in fact the form the audience knows better.

Manage pace as a design variable: the speaker controls it, too fast loses the audience and too slow bores them, and the speaker's own sense of their pace is unreliable — so calibrate it from the audience or from an observer, not from how it feels.
Discount perceived quality for delivery in both directions when judging a talk or a speaker, since a poor delivery makes work look weaker than it is and an exceptional one makes it look stronger.

Treat delivery — voice, gestures, eye contact, stance, and movement — as determining not only how intently the audience listens but whether they trust the speaker, since an audience engages with any subject only when it is delivered engagingly.
Treat remote delivery as a degraded channel: teleconferencing solves audience assembly but not energy, and recording loses the audience interaction that makes a presentation worth giving.

An effortless, conversational delivery is the product of dogged preparation across many script revisions, and rehearsal can extend to anticipating multiple audience reactions with alternate sections written for each, plus notation of where and how the presenter will stand.

Treat presenting as a research activity, not only a reporting one: cross-disciplinary questions yield new perspectives on the work, and preparing the talk solidifies the speaker's own ideas and can produce new insights.

Critique a talk from four separate perspectives — speech, structure, visual aids, and delivery — while remembering that strength in one can offset weakness in another; the decisive test is whether a weak area distracts the audience from the content.

Test each detail of a known audience's talk against two questions — will they understand it, and will they be interested in it — and when the audience is unknown, mingle beforehand to ask what work people do, why they came, and what they know, or else try the talk on someone with the same background.

Treat post-talk reflection as part of the work, since a subject presented once will usually be presented again: audience questions mark the points the body explained badly, and what the audience failed to notice is as informative as what they responded to.

Improve delivery through deliberate cycles of reflection and revision — cutting the notes, slowing the tempo, then actively querying the audience about the result — and shorten those cycles by having colleagues critique what was strong as well as weak and by reviewing a recording of oneself critically.
Read audience praise cautiously, since it may reflect modest expectations rather than a successful talk, and expect a speaker's self-criticism to grow harsher rather than softer as they improve.

Walk through the whole presentation beforehand even in a mumble, because practice smooths the transitions between assertions, works out the explanations of difficult concepts, and above all dispels the greatest source of a speaker's nervousness — the fear of standing before an audience with nothing to say.

Prepare a second-language talk on four extra fronts — enriching the field's vocabulary, practising the pronunciation of its common words, using assertion-evidence slides that hand the audience each takeaway with visual support, and preparing podium notes for when a word goes missing — recognising that memorising the talk is not enough because questions must be understood and answered on the spot, and arranging for a colleague in the audience where listening comprehension is weak.

Choose reading where every word will be examined — a press conference, a welcome address, or a management talk on a controversial issue — and then make it work on three conditions: every idea in the text counts and the sentences are engaging and often surprising, the wording is precise with pleasing rhythms, and the speaker has practised enough to look up, keep a natural pace, and pause for emphasis.

Recognise the two failure modes of composure: stage fright severe enough to reduce the talk to a fast reading nobody understands well enough to question, and the mid-talk spiral in which a question trips the speaker, confidence drops, the audience senses a flaw and presses, and the questions turn more biting.

Read a bad case of nerves as a signal of insufficient preparation and answer it with two or three full practice runs with the visual aids, timing any colleague's critique early enough that valid criticisms can be worked in, since major changes just before a talk can do more harm than good.

Critique a presentation from multiple perspectives, naming both what was strong and what could be stronger, while recognising that not every criterion applies to every talk and that team presentations need additional ones.

Check content and speech against three criteria — whether the audience was targeted, the purpose achieved, and the occasion met — and the beginning against four: scope given, importance shown, background and credibility established, and mapping made memorable.

Impress the audience with the content rather than the style, but never neglect style: it is the vehicle that carries the content, so content without style goes unnoticed and style without content means nothing.

Strip allusions and references outside the audience's shared background, slow the pace, and make the connections between points explicit — the combination of obscure reference and excessive speed is what drives listeners away.
Recover a tiring audience by stepping closer, lifting the pace and volume, and drawing explicit connections between the content and the listeners' own work.

Emphasise deliberately, because listeners remember only a fraction of what they hear and a well-organised talk without emphasis leaves them carrying away its least important details; the available mechanisms are repetition, illustration, and placement, plus the delivery moves of pausing, changing volume — often lowering it — and stepping closer.

Move quickly from the general to the specific without detouring onto side paths, and resist the drive for completeness in which each mentioned detail drags in another the audience was never prepared for.

Map the talk explicitly, because a reader can glance ahead at headings while a listener cannot, and a clear memorable map is what lets the audience pace themselves; use images repeated in the corresponding divisions and omit generic entries such as Introduction and Conclusion.
Match what is said to the audience, the purpose, and the occasion, since failing any one of the three is what constitutes giving the wrong speech.
Hold a scientific talk to both standards at once — precise and engaging — because a technically correct talk that loses the audience's attention communicates nothing.

Prepare a general-public talk against one specific non-scientist the speaker knows well, imagining that person saying 'I don't get it' or 'So what?', because the public is too varied in education and interest to address as a whole — and a single well-made public talk can transform the presenter's reach.
Aim higher than the staid presentation style most scientists and engineers resign themselves to, crafting for the given audience, purpose, and occasion a talk genuinely worth the audience's time.
Anticipate the decision-makers' prior bias before building a persuasive case, because a technically sound argument can fail against an audience under pressure to decide the other way.
Build a persuasive scientific case from all three appeals — logical evidence, appeals to the audience's emotion, and appeals to the speaker's own character — rather than logic alone.

Assess the audience's prior bias first, because it sets both the strategy and the energy an argument requires and can be the overriding determinant of the outcome regardless of the speaker's stature — the same argument succeeding with one audience and failing with another on bias alone.
Identify the mix of purposes before crafting the speech, since few scientific presentations only inform: most also persuade, and some also aim to inspire.
Let the mix of purposes determine how the speech is crafted, since most presentations carry more than one.

State the slide's assertion explicitly and show the one variable it depends on: a slide whose assertion is implicit, whose evidence is buried in irrelevant detail, and whose decisive variable is missing cannot carry the argument no matter how much data it holds.

Diagnose a failed persuasive slide by its missing assertion: where the assertion is left implicit and the slide body never shows the relationship the argument rests on, writing the assertion as the headline would itself have driven the speaker to find the right evidence.

Treat the sentence assertion as a safety net for any listener who missed the spoken transition into the slide, and convert the projected deck into a handout by putting the secondary details on the notes pages rather than on the slides.
Make clarity the overriding principle for any data on a slide, because projected data cannot be pulled close and examined the way print can.
Include data on a slide only when it illustrates the conclusion, and render it so it is absorbable from the back of the room, because a cluttered data slide can derail even a compelling speaker.
Confirm rather than assume who will be in the room, and expect targeting to get harder as the audience gets less technical, because more terms and more background must then be anticipated.
Match both the channel and the post-presentation material to how this audience prefers to receive information, including room setup and what they take away.

Retarget the same material for a new audience by varying the examples, the depth, and the background supplied rather than rewriting it, and rehearse mentally by imagining the audience's reaction to each assertion and each piece of evidence.
Rehearse and plan the memorable moments, because the presentations that get repeated carry moments engineered to hold the right balance of analytical and emotional appeal.

Rehearse repeatedly in front of the actual audience profile, incorporating feedback each round, and expect the "change nothing" verdict only near the end of a long sequence of rehearsals rather than after the first few.

Do not present the intricacies of the work at full density to a mixed audience: listeners outside the discipline dismiss genuinely important results they cannot follow, and reaching a mixed audience is harder than reaching a single one.

Serve the three sub-audiences of a mixed room on their own terms: specialists expect depth in the specialty demonstrated somewhere in the talk, other-field researchers need the significance shown explicitly and want insights connecting to their own work, and non-technical decision-makers need a connection made to them because they may control the funding.

Abandon the goal of satisfying a mixed audience throughout the whole talk — no design achieves it — and aim instead for everyone satisfied by the end, addressing the different audiences at different moments.
Do not omit orienting material for fear of boring the specialists: presenting what part of the audience already knows does not bore them provided the explanation is done well.

Design against the three specific ways audiences get lost — gaps in the logic they cannot bridge, an unsignalled change of direction, and exhaustion from too many details — and assume listeners will drift even with sound structure, so build in a way for them to recover.

Engineer contrast against the audience's own environment and expectations, because obscurity rather than opposition is what defeats an idea and nothing carries intrinsic attention-grabbing power apart from how far it stands out from its context.

Segment the audience and target the subsegment offering the greatest impact for the least effort, accepting that appealing broadly while connecting deeply with that subset is difficult but worth the effort.
Deliberately alternate approaches so different listeners are caught on different hooks and no segment of a mixed audience is bored throughout.
An audience will not adopt an idea it does not understand, and the idea's perceived value is judged less on its merit than on how well it is communicated.

Find a way to connect with non-technical officials and managers in the room, because they typically grasp neither the significance of the work nor the theory behind it yet may have the largest say in whether it is funded.

Use a shallow-to-deep-to-shallow depth profile for a mixed audience: open shallow enough to orient everyone and show rather than state the importance, begin each middle division in the shallows before diving, and return to the shallows at the end so every listener leaves with the main points.

Set depth from what the audience needs or wants: assess what they already know, begin the discussion there, and account for how much more they need to learn — recognising the judgment gets markedly harder with multiple audiences.

When a recognised expert on a sub-topic is in the room, name them, concede they could explain it better, and then present as well as possible — which tends to recruit them as an ally and makes any correction they offer a kind one.

For an instructional talk whose credentials the audience accepts, deliver the information as logically and directly as possible with emphasis on warnings and key steps — the one occasion where the preview-tell-summarize structure genuinely serves, and where an audience acting under pressure wants the how rather than the why.

Orient the audience even at the risk of seeming simplistic: attendees do not expect to understand everything but do expect to understand something for the time invested, and opening as though they had read all the speaker's papers fails them.
Plan explicitly what the presentation gives the audience — guidance to navigate the journey, confidence so they are not reluctant, and tools they take with them.

Match the evidence budget to the logical shape of the assertion: a universal positive claim requires showing every criterion is met, while a negative claim requires showing only that one fails — so prefer the assertion the available evidence can actually carry.

Recognise compromise as a legitimate goal of a persuasive presentation: not every one must move the audience to the speaker's position, and negotiating a compromise can convert a competitive situation into a productive collaboration.

Treat every presentation as persuasive and state explicitly what shift it must produce in the audience, since even a nominally informative talk moves people from uninformed to informed or from inaction to action.

If no audience transformation is required, write and distribute a report instead of presenting — while recognizing that routine-looking meetings often do contain a persuasive situation that demands a defined journey.

In teaching, prefer letting students discover a principle over telling it to them, since discovered material is more likely to be owned — while accepting that several methods work for any subject and audience and at least as many fail, and that methods out of place in a business talk can succeed in a classroom.

Read the occasion as a set of concrete variables — formality, time limit, time of day, logistics, location, and number of attendees — and design against them rather than against a generic notion of the event.

Treat a fixed time limit as hard when others are waiting to speak, and let the time of day temper how ambitious the talk is, since a late-afternoon audience absorbs fewer main points than a mid-morning one.

Watch for the self-defeating loop in which anxiety about the time limit accelerates the speaker, and treat unanimous audience agreement on a delivery fault as a strong signal, since at least one listener in most audiences is too polite to criticise.

Split the time before a major talk into two phases: meet the audience early to learn who they are, what motivates them, and what they know about the work, then withdraw alone in the final hours to rehearse the route through the talk calmly — a quiet block that is essential even for a talk already given several times, taken the night before or early that morning if the schedule forbids it later.

Impose a shorter time constraint than the slot allows — given an hour, target forty minutes — because restricting time forces clear structure and filters content down to imperative messages, and a shorter talk demands more preparation rather than less.
Keep a formal or very short talk tight to the targeted subject, and reserve examples, stories, humour, and personal connections for informal occasions or generous time budgets.

Recognise that a run of bulleted lists bores an audience for a structural reason, not a cosmetic one: the volume of listed details overwhelms while the format hides both the connections and the relative importance among them, leaving no anchor for understanding and no mnemonic for recall.
Where a list is genuinely unavoidable, keep it short and present it as a sequence of images or a short table rather than as bullets.

Recognise the ease of bulleted lists as their real danger: they let the speaker skip deciding how the details relate, requiring only parallel grammar, so a list is brainstorming dressed as a finished presentation — surface thinking that should be a presenter's last choice, not their first.

Allow a long list only where the audience is not expected to read it but to see that many instances exist, and grade the type contrast from dark for the most serious items to light for the least so the list reads as an image rather than as text to be worked through.

Make technical content stick through four devices — stories, examples and analogies, a personal connection with the audience, and humour — with humour admitted only when it arises naturally from the content and offends no one.

Use stories for two specific jobs — creating the anticipation that makes an audience lean in, and supplying the frame that lets them recall the sequence of details hours later — while keeping the talk a blend of document and story rather than a story outright.

Maintain a personal catalogue of stories indexed by emotion, recalling them not only by life chronology but by people, places and things, sketching the scene to surface dormant memories and recording how the presenter felt as each unfolded.

Structure a scientific story by stating the hypothesis up front, ordering details so tension builds, breaking from the narrative to explain the science, releasing the tension at the answer, and foreshadowing the next question during that build-up so the middle can sustain more than one peak.

Anchor any concept the audience does not know in an example or an analogy, since a purely abstract or mathematical treatment loses most listeners who need an image or physical perspective — and attaching a physical example to a derivation can even expose errors that listeners tracking only the algebra would miss.
Ground the problem in a specific physical example rather than discussing the technique in the abstract, because that is what carries much of the audience through the mathematical stretches.

Reach for an analogy specifically to convey the scale of something unfamiliar or the likelihood of an unfamiliar event, since vivid comparisons that genuinely support the content are what the audience carries out of the room.

Use analogies to explain how something works or how large it is, not to support an assertion in an argument, because an analogy ties two dissimilar things from one narrow perspective and a skeptical audience can attack the differences visible from any other.
Test a presentation's success by what the audience still remembers two days later, not by how it felt in the room.
A recorded presentation transcends the moment it was given and can reach far more people than were present, so a message that is clear and worth repeating will be repeated.
Restate numbers in terms the audience already experiences — capacity as a count of familiar items, size as fitting in a pocket — rather than in raw technical units.

Build a personal connection through eye contact, humility, evident concern that everyone understands, an account of what motivated the work, and openness about the difficulty and opposition met — all of which connect where speaking to impress does not.

Require three things of the speaker in a strong presentation — understanding the subject well enough that what is imparted is worth the audience's time, showing genuine enthusiasm for it, and holding a keen awareness of what the audience knows, what will engage them, and what biases they carry — while accepting that no speaker knows everything or needs exceptional charisma, only that they instil a respect for the subject.

Name the individuals in the audience whose work connects to the speaker's — and learn listeners' names in a teaching setting — because doing so signals respect, recruits experts as allies, raises concentration, and increases the speaker's credibility.

Name the presenters and sponsors and show familiarity with the key players in the research area, because both answer what the audience needs in order to believe the subject rather than merely understand it.
Earn the audience's trust by respecting them first — never displaying superiority and leaving listeners free to question and criticise — because an effective speaker must be liked and trusted.

Treat humour as a high-variance instrument: it can relax, engage, and rest an audience, but landing a line depends on pausing, timing, and emphasis that not every speaker has, and attempts before an unfamiliar professional audience often draw groans.

Do not open a talk with a joke: humour depends on violating an expectation the audience has not yet formed of an unknown speaker, the speaker is most nervous at that moment, and a failure lands exactly when the audience is sizing them up — so place humour in the middle, once credibility exists.

Never plan humour: let it emerge from the material and the audience's mood, back off and play the talk straight if a first attempt draws nothing, and prefer self-effacing jokes about the speaker's own failings.
Weigh the standing cost of being the funny speaker: listeners begin reading jokes into statements meant seriously.

Accept that no humour is safe for everyone: a remark that works over an informal lunch reads as crass in a formal meeting, controversial subjects irritate rather than relax, someone in any large professional audience is sensitive to race, gender, religion, or death, and sexual remarks are out of bounds.

Do not expect content and delivery to rescue failed structure and visual aids: an interesting topic delivered energetically still empties a room when it runs to dozens of bulleted slides with each point animated in one at a time.

Design slides for the audience rather than as the speaker's notes, because projecting one's own speaking points produces the robotic cycle of turning to the screen for each bullet and back to the room for a sentence.

Treat TED-style simplicity as engineered rather than effortless: it costs more preparation than assertion-evidence slides and demands artistic judgment in cropping and placement, and it is achieved by concrete moves — raising the signal-to-noise ratio, eliminating unneeded text and lines, using empty space deliberately, and building scenes rather than slides.
Use a writing board rather than projected bulleted slides when the goal is generating ideas in a discussion.
Repair the message before the visuals; improving slide design cannot rescue content that is meaningless.

Accept that fewer slides can be stronger: storytelling, large gestures, and one memorable physical object can outperform media, with the few slides used only to supply context — the method is instrumental to the outcome, not a value in itself.

Cover two or three aspects of a subject rather than every one, because a scope that wide forces a depth so shallow that every point becomes generic and no room remains for the stories and examples that hold attention — and never announce a long enumerated list late in a talk.

Deliver satisfying depth inside a deliberately broad talk rather than avoiding breadth: spread concrete and simple stories and examples across the scope, or group the topics into two or three memorable categories and go deep on one example from each.

Design structure on four levers, any one of which can fail a talk: the organisation itself, the number of changes in direction, the signalling of those changes, and the emphasis of key details — and against four pitfalls: doing too much, losing the audience at the beginning, losing them in the middle, and not being persuasive enough.

Open with the big picture, narrow to the topic, treat it logically in the middle, and return in the ending to how the work bears on the big picture — analysing the work overall, summarising its most important details, and closing with recommendations, unresolved questions, or its effect on that big picture.

Put something important in the beginning — the scope, the importance of the work, or the single most important result — because the audience is least tired and listening most sharply there; but open with the result only when it strikes the audience as positive or neutral and they understand and appreciate it.

Derive the middle's ordering from the kind of topic — chronological for a process, spatial for an object, flow-following for a system, parallel grouping for a classifiable topic — unless audience expectations impose one, as a research audience expects hypotheses, then how they were tested, then results.
Treat illogical organisation as costing future audiences, not just this one: listeners who cannot follow the structure stop attending that speaker's talks.
Never announce a decision to a hostile audience and address their concerns afterwards: the reassurance arrives too late, listeners stop listening, and the meeting is lost.

Limit the middle to two, three, or four divisions, because listeners process lists of that size and larger ones tax them; a list of six to nine items should be broken into two or three categories the audience can hold.

Hold any grouping on a slide to four items or fewer, since audiences remember groupings of two, three, and four and forget larger ones — placing only the three or four most important call-outs on a photograph and folding the rest into speech, or folding an equally weighted long list into two or three memorable categories with the members named aloud.

Signal every transition through at least one of three channels — the wording of the speech, a change in the visual aids, or the delivery — at all the points that need it: introduction to middle, between each pair of middle sections, and middle to conclusion.

Pair analytical devices with emotional ones in the same talk: signal the structure up front and mark transitions, announce how many points are coming, use visuals sparingly alongside gesture, and interleave wonderment and subject-related humour at roughly even intervals.

Mark the transition into the conclusion unmistakably, because listeners who know only a minute or two remains sit up and attend more closely, and a speaker who instead ends abruptly with a bare request for questions denies the audience the chance to view the work as a whole and lowers the odds they remember its important details.

Leave the conclusion slide projected through the question period rather than a question mark or the word Questions, since it is on screen for minutes and should be carrying the presentation's most important results.

Make the beginning as clear as possible, because a listener lost there wastes the whole session when questions are deferred or the room is too large to ask — and the two hallmarks of that failure are a title slide flashed away before anyone grasps the subject and an outline list nobody can recall a minute later.
Target the beginning at the widest possible audience, so that even listeners lost in the middle can afterwards tell a colleague in general terms what was done and why it mattered.
Prepare the audience patiently for the problems to be discussed rather than rushing into details on the assumption that they know the subject as well as the speaker does.

Spend more than twenty or thirty seconds on the title slide and answer at least one of the audience's opening questions before the first slide change — which a key image on that slide makes possible by giving the speaker an entry point — because reading off title, name, affiliation, date, and logos and then switching leaves all four unanswered while the audience is still adjusting to the speaker.

Be most patient at the opening when the speaker is junior and carries no credibility yet, because the audience is actively judging whether the talk will waste their time and must be shown up front that it will not.

State up front what knowledge is being assumed when the time limit prevents supplying all the background, because listeners who lack it can then set realistic expectations and relax, which may leave them understanding more than if they had tried to follow every step.

Run a closing sequence that gives the audience time to compose questions: a headline beginning 'In closing' or 'In summary' so they start as the slide appears, a strong final sentence, a pause for applause with a thank-you to cue it if none comes, and only then the word Questions animated in — because an abrupt ending produces silence that reads as though nobody understood or cared.

Answer a question after a deliberate pause, which buys time to consider and lends emphasis to the answer's first sentence, since audiences are far more patient with visible silent thought than with empty chatter or filler words.

Listen to the question, because the relief of finishing the last slide makes it easy to miss the first one entirely — and treat question periods as opportunities that deliver feedback from colleagues seeing the work with fresh eyes rather than as threats.

Stay the leader when the audience can interrupt: postpone premature questions the talk will reach later and decline out-of-scope ones with an offer to discuss them afterwards, which most questioners accept when the refusal is diplomatic.
Keep the beginning to roughly ten percent of total time or less, because the audience is impatient to learn why they are there and what is being proposed.

Budget for the cost of a speaker change in a group presentation — a new voice, stage presence, and set of movements to adjust to — so that occasional handovers give a long talk variety while too many in a short talk cause confusion.

Let the projected deck and the documenting handout differ: a viewer reads a slide while the speaker talks at 120 to 140 words a minute, whereas a handout is read afterwards at the reader's own pace, and forcing the two to match is what locks presenters into projecting far too many words.

Price the cost of default-following slides correctly: they are cheap to make the night before, but slide design shapes three separate things — how the speaker prepares, how the speaker delivers, and how much the audience understands and remembers.

Budget preparation across three fronts — understanding the content well enough to organise it comprehensibly, gathering images and graphing results into well-designed slides, and rehearsing to find the words for difficult concepts and smooth the transitions — because young researchers systematically underestimate what good talks cost.
Make the logical strategy of the middle identifiable and recallable by the audience, whatever strategy is chosen, because that is what holds retention through it.
Overcome the Curse of Knowledge by stepping away from the work and viewing each assertion as the audience will, since an expert cannot recall what it was like not to know what they know.

Balance scope against depth as a fixed-volume trade for a fixed talk length: a wide scope raises the chance something connects but lowers achievable depth, a narrow one deepens the treatment but risks not connecting at all — and where the occasion fixes the scope, the depth must be adjusted rather than the reverse.

State out loud what the talk is excluding, anticipating the omission the audience would otherwise puzzle over — the practice of strong presenters, and the opposite of the insecure presenter who covers as much as possible to impress the audience or to deter questions.

Practise short impromptu talks anyway, because question periods force off-the-cuff speaking on both the presenter answering and the audience member asking, and that practice builds the confidence those moments demand.

Define the audience accurately and appropriately for the specific presentation, avoiding clichéd or over-broad segmentation that makes the presenter seem unprepared and can leave the audience feeling stereotyped or reduced to a statistic.

Edit severely on the audience's behalf, because presentation quality depends as much on what is removed as on what is included and an unfiltered talk makes the audience work too hard to find what matters — a failure they can now broadcast publicly.

Select, sort, and rank the details: keep only those that let the audience understand the work, order them so no on-the-spot cataloguing is needed, and give them a hierarchy — including stating the essentials up front — so listeners know which to hold onto and which to release when overwhelmed.

Ensure that none of the audience's four opening questions — what the subject is, why it is important, what is needed to understand or believe it, and in what order it will be presented — remains open once the introduction ends, though not all four need be addressed explicitly for an audience that already knows some answers.

Open by stating what is — a concise formulation of what everyone agrees is true about the current or historical situation — because accurately capturing the audience's reality proves the presenter understands their context and values, creates a common bond, and supplies the baseline without which the new idea has no dramatic effect.

Scale the introduction to the slot — up to ten minutes in a fifty-minute talk, no more than five in a fifteen-minute conference presentation — because an overlong introduction makes the audience impatient and a long opening story leads many to assume the speaker has little to report.

Meet the deadline in an uninterrupted talk by preparation: define a scope coverable in the time allotted and plan no more slides than that time allows, respecting soak time — 20 slides for a 15-minute talk makes no sense outside a Lessig sequence, a title slide deserves about 60 seconds, and a complex graphic needs more still.

Constrain the length hard, because attention spans are short and constraint forces the presenter to be concise and cut anything superfluous — the world's most influential talks land in eighteen minutes or less, and a fixed format such as twenty slides at twenty seconds each forces ruthless self-editing.

Cap the presentation portion of an internal meeting and reserve time for conversation, collaboration, and Q&A, because cramming more content than the slot allows produces an auctioneer pace and forces the presenter to dodge questions.

Do not rely on the posted title and abstract to have oriented the audience: they were read hours or days earlier, people retain little of what they read, and the spoken review adds emphasis through loudness and cadence that text cannot.

Do not enter the middle of a talk until the audience understands why the subject matters — usually a thirty- to forty-second connection to money, safety, health, or the environment, or, where the work has no practical payoff, the transfer of the speaker's own curiosity — because listening is hard work that audiences abandon without sufficient reason.

Assume the audience carries an unspoken fear of not understanding and will not ask for clarification even when permitted, for fear of appearing ignorant or distracting others — so the speaker must remove the need to ask.

Discount the fear of an unanswerable question, since the audience does not expect the speaker to know everything and many questions fall outside the talk's scope — which should be said plainly while still connecting the question to something the speaker does know.

Distribute background deliberately: signal in the introduction what background is coming, put the work's major assumptions up front, deliver the rest as needed, and move a block long enough to feel like its own section into the middle only if that does not over-section it and the relationship stays visible.
Keep everything in the background subordinate to the content and keep photographs out of the background entirely, because the audience will spend effort decoding a partially obscured image.

Distinguish the two kinds of background — what the audience needs to understand the subject and what they need to believe it — and supply the second deliberately as institution, colleagues, and the literature the work builds on.

Divide the talk into sections, know roughly how long each runs, and rehearse the entries and exits while leaving the interiors unrehearsed — producing genuine spontaneity inside a structure that prevents the wandering that can consume the time and leave the planned structure undelivered.

Build a repertoire of four-to-five-minute segments given many times, select which segments a given talk will use, and spend the preparation on the transitions into and out of each — a workable route to note-free speaking.

Keep controlling the room during the talk — shutting a noisy door, mitigating an early departure by looking to the opposite side, and stopping entirely when outside noise makes hearing impossible — because the speaker cannot control the disturbance but can control the reaction, and a well-practised speaker can carry on from memory through a total lighting failure and even turn the incident to advantage.

Structure the presentation around two turning points — the call to adventure separating the beginning from the middle, and the call to action separating the middle from the end — and extend the form past the talk to the subsequent action the audience performs after leaving.
Memorize a talk as a mental building whose rooms carry the ideas, so the story survives any route through it — fixing the visual aids in one tour order when they are used.

Present topics the speaker actually understands, since a speaker who cannot see the destination cannot lead the audience there; presenting settled material reads as lucid while presenting material still being grappled with reads as groping.

Own the misunderstanding when a presentation is misread: the presenter chose the words and images, and a message pitched at an urgency the audience has never lived through reads as manipulation rather than insight.

Mark explicitly which claims are solidly grounded in theory and experiment and which are the speaker's own suspicions, whatever mix the talk carries — a bold claim that proves wrong invites public embarrassment while a right one earns credit a cautious colleague forgoes, and only the labelling makes that gamble honest.

Set the speculative content by audience, purpose, and occasion: stay with facts before a funder or any audience where a stumble cannot be afforded, and reserve the deliberately provisional straw-man — which turns the audience into a source of the answer — for colleagues with whom credibility is established.

Feature rather than downplay a result the speaker cannot yet explain: state up front that it is not understood and make the search for its explanation an emphasis of the talk, because a downplayed result is both excluded from the audience's decisions and exposed during questions, where listeners gravitate to exactly what they did not understand.

Close each division and name the next in speech, reserving phrases such as 'in summary' or 'to conclude' for the shift into the ending, and reinforce the boundary with a repeated corner icon from the mapping slide so the audience has a continuous wordless signal of where they are.

Set layout to guide the eye: text blocks and especially headlines to no more than two lines, any list or set of call-outs to two, three, or four items, animation only where it serves the audience and never gimmicky, and enough blank space between elements that the slide breathes.

Cut a mapping list to the order of the divisions alone — dropping Introduction and Conclusion, acknowledgements and questions fixed by the occasion, background coverable beforehand, and sub-methods not needed yet — and never let a bulleted list do the mapping, which is close to the least memorable form it could take.

Make the map memorable by integrating the divisions into a single image that also supplies the background, or, failing that, by anchoring each topic with a representative image — a large body of experiments found an audience twice as likely to recall a topic anchored that way — and repeat each anchoring image on the first slide of its division.

Use the pause as a working instrument: audiences read it as the speaker collecting their thoughts rather than being lost, and it gives them the room to sort, synthesize, and analyse what was just delivered — alongside the other delivery signals of counting the division on the fingers, changing vocal level, moving closer, taking a fixed position, and repeating a consistent ritual motion between segments.

Start persuasion by recognising exactly what is being asserted and by fixing the main assertion the data supports before deciding how to graph or present it, because an audience believes an argument far more readily when they know and appreciate its assertions and because every detail spoken and shown should then drive toward that assertion.

Build a chain of evidenced sub-assertions when the main assertion sits too far up the mountain for one graph or dataset to reach, fitting each sub-assertion's evidence to its kind of claim, and supply the background warrants without which the audience cannot appreciate the assertion even while following every word.

Build a data slide about the meaning of the data rather than the data itself, and articulate the conclusion the audience should adopt — usually a causal point — before choosing the chart, because that conclusion determines the graph type and the emphasis.

Account for all three appeals — logic, the audience's emotion, and the speaker's own character — rather than logic alone, because scientists systematically underrate the other two and because many political decisions about science are made by non-technical people whom character and emotion sway.
Cover all three Aristotelian appeals — ethical, emotional and logical — because facts alone do not persuade and must be complemented by credibility and by content that reaches the heart.

Rank logical evidence by strength when selecting support — deductive reasoning, then inductive, then referenced facts, then statistics, then examples, with analogies weakest — and prefer the strongest form the material allows.

Judge a statistic by whether the quantities compared are actually comparable: experimental data showing a definite trend persuades, while a comparison that ignores the variables differing between the two quantities does not.

Match an example's logical force to the assertion it supports: one instance of harm is powerful evidence that something is dangerous, while one instance without side effects is weak evidence that it is safe.

Build the character appeal deliberately: recognised authority carries a claim further than an unknown speaker can, a speaker without eminent credentials can make a position that runs counter to their own record part of the evidence, and reputation is earned by showing not only that one's own result is right but why the conflicting result is wrong.
Set realistic aims with an antagonistic audience — reducing the opposition's vehemence and winning the neutrals, not converting opponents — since important innovations rarely convert theirs.
Plan for the audience to resist and raise obstacles, and acknowledge the struggle openly rather than presenting the change as painless.

Against an antagonistic audience, define the question up front while withholding the results so the speaker's position stays unknown and opponents actually listen, and open by demonstrating genuine understanding of the opposition's strongest arguments before mounting any defence.

Concede publicly when a challenger is right — stating plainly that the questioner is correct and that the work beyond that step is wrong — since holding one's ground need not create animosity and the willingness to admit being wrong is the clearest sign of a speaker's security and marks their aim as truth rather than personal glory.

Blank the screen for any stretch of the talk that gains nothing from a slide — via a black slide, the blank button, or the B key — which moves the focus from the screen's light to the speaker; personal stories and acknowledgements are the natural occasions.

Make the final projected slide summarise the talk's most important takeaway, because it is displayed longest while questions are taken and it gives the audience content from which to fashion questions; an empty one is worse than a blank screen, a Thank You slide wastes the screen when voice and expression convey the thanks better, and a Questions slide tells the audience what they already know.
Blank the projector when it is not needed, which removes the glare and frees the speaker to occupy the part of the room otherwise in the projected light.

Blank the screen deliberately with the black or white key, or with an inserted black slide when the keyboard is out of reach, because a pause creates drama and meaning, gives the audience time to contemplate, and makes them feel they are interacting solely with the presenter.

Treat the presentation software's defaults as an unvalidated inheritance rather than guidance: they were never founded on research, originated when embedding graphics was hard, shape the overwhelming majority of scientific slides through sheer market share, and are repeated in the alternative masters two navigation levels deep.

Assess every software default against the actual audience, purpose, and occasion and change proactively what does not serve them, rather than either following the defaults or avoiding the software — noting that weak practices spawned by those defaults are baked into institutional templates that leave younger practitioners unaware alternatives exist.

Judge a headline type by which one leads the speaker to prepare a more focused talk with fewer words overall and which better re-orients a listener who missed the transition onto the slide — not by which is shorter.

Reject the bulleted list on three grounds at once: it does not show connections, does not reveal hierarchy, and leaves the critical assertions unspecified — while its word count makes reading and listening simultaneously difficult and its position squeezes out the space for graphics.

Measure a slide against projected words per minute rather than against a per-slide word rule, because a slide projected for about a minute competes with the 120 to 140 words the speaker delivers in that same minute — which is why even a 6-by-6-compliant slide carries too many words.

Avoid the cognitive-overload condition in which comprehension falls below what it would have been with no slides at all: spoken and written words are processed by the same channel, so an over-worded slide leaves the listener only the three bad options of ignoring the screen, tuning out the speaker, or toggling between them.

Follow the body rules concretely: support the headline with visual evidence — photographs, drawings, diagrams, graphs, films, equations, or short tables — use words only where necessary, and hold the design to no more than 20 projected words per minute.

Limit animation stages to four per slide unless the aim is deliberately to overwhelm, and never attach sounds to a slide build, since clicks, whooshes, and screeching brakes have no place in a professional presentation.

Put only a small fraction of the spoken sentences on the slides — roughly one projected sentence for every ten spoken — because projecting a large share splits the audience three ways, none of which serves comprehension.

Answer the risk of groping for a word with repeated practice rather than with a script, since a scientific audience does not expect an actor's fluency and properly spaced pauses actually emphasise key points — and where exact wording genuinely matters, such as a law or a difficult definition, put that wording on the slide or in discreet notes without abandoning extemporaneous delivery.

Reject memorisation at presentation length: at roughly 130 to 140 words a minute a 15-minute talk means memorising over 2,000 words, the result cannot be changed mid-stream — forfeiting one of the main reasons for presenting rather than documenting — and it recalls words faster than an audience can absorb them.

Never read large portions of the text off a projected slide, because the audience reads ahead or guesses the gist so surprise is destroyed and both parties end up looking at the screen instead of each other — the one exception being a Lessig-style sequence rehearsed deeply enough that short phrases appear at or just after the moment they are spoken.

Practise the whole presentation with the slides to build confidence both that the words will come and that the talk fits the limit, and correct for the fact that rehearsal timing does not transfer directly — nervousness makes most speakers faster before a live audience while a few become slower.

Reject the slide application's default report-shaped master, since a text-filled default slide takes about twenty-five seconds to read and forty of them spend over sixteen minutes with the audience reading instead of listening.

Plan the structure against the time frame to guarantee staying inside the slot, and never treat slide count as a proxy for duration — there is no right number of slides, since the count follows the presenter's pacing.

Apply an explicit word-count boundary when auditing a slide: past roughly 75 words it is a document, and around 50 words it is functioning as a teleprompter — move the text into the notes or reclassify the artifact.

Keep the word count low enough to serve only as a mnemonic the presenter is comfortable delivering, because a wordy slide is read faster than it can be explained and makes the presenter irrelevant to their own presentation — recognizing that the application's default template is already a document, not a visual aid.
Use bullets sparingly if at all and reject prescriptive counting rules such as 4x4, 5x5, or seven words per slide in favour of composing the slide with design sense.

Choose the slide count from the delivery style and message rather than a rule — one slide every two minutes is only the common default, a fast one-big-idea-per-slide style can run to hundreds and needs practice, others linger minutes per slide — while keeping one point per slide because anything more demands more than most audiences will give.

Choose the assertion-evidence structure on its two stated grounds — it follows the psychology of how people learn and it is designed for communicating technical assertions — while recognising that other grounded structures exist for less technical content.

Present the evidence before the assertion in three situations — teaching, a complex assertion, and a skeptical audience — showing evidence under a question headline in a classroom before animating in the answer, delaying a complex assertion until the visual evidence has been explained and then leaving the slide up for soak time, and withholding a controversial assertion so the evidence lands before the naysayers compose their rebuttal.

Treat the comprehension advantage of assertion-evidence slides as measured rather than asserted: a controlled comparison holding the narrated speech constant, against a conservative baseline better than common practice, found significantly higher comprehension and retention with the essay test reaching p < .01, and the gain corresponds to one and sometimes two letter grades.

Expect assertion-evidence slides to improve delivery in three specific ways — more eye contact because the assertion is absorbed into natural speech, more natural speech because words are fashioned on the spot to explain images, and an appearance of greater confidence because the information plainly comes from the speaker — and note that the audience follows the speaker's gaze to an explained image where the reading-aloud pattern pushes them away.

Expect three returns from the assertion-evidence structure — better audience comprehension, a better speaker-audience connection because the speaker no longer turns to read points off the slides, and most importantly a more focused talk — the focus coming from identifying the main takeaways and then using them as the filter for selecting supporting evidence.
Never animate bullets in one at a time: much of the audience stops watching the animations and either watches the speaker read or disengages entirely.

Reveal content progressively and hide each element until it is referred to — including greying out already-covered items on a recurring agenda slide — because viewers read a visual the instant it appears, so exposed bullets or several simultaneous visuals split the audience between listening and reading ahead.

Plan for slow adoption of a better slide structure: professionals convert over a long period through interest, doubt, experimentation, and conversion, held back both by entrenched institutional templates and by the genuine difficulty of defining the key assertions and building the visual evidence.

Give a collaborative presentation extra preparation time with one person owning slide creation for a consistent format and a deck that reveals the organisation, while everyone meets early to shape the story, contributes visual evidence, and comments on a draft.

Follow the headline rules concretely: no more than two lines, left justified, capitalised as a sentence with the period optional, starting in the upper-left corner where Western audiences look first, set at 28 points, and broken so that noun, verb, and prepositional phrases stay together with no single word orphaned on the second line.

Set typography for reading speed: a sans serif face boldfaced for larger rooms, 28 point headline, 18 to 24 point body, 12 to 14 point reference listings, and no italics, underlining, or all capitals.

Choose the typeface by reading speed rather than tradition, since the audience reads while listening: sans serif faces read faster in the short blocks of a slide, their straighter strokes matter most for viewers at a sharp side angle, and the penalty for a serif face becomes decisive when the projector or room lighting is poor.

Prefer a sans serif face that is present on most computers — an advantage when loading a deck onto a meeting-room machine — and a narrower one, which leaves more blank space at the edges of a text block.

Boldface slide type, especially for a larger room, and avoid italics and underlining: italics are too slow to read when projected, particularly from side angles, and the underscore adds noise that impairs letter recognition.

Set colour to serve the audience and the room: dark type on a light background or light type on a dark one, no hot background colours, no decorated backgrounds, and no logo allowed to detract from the content.

Reject stock decorated backgrounds as pure noise that also consumes area — one popular background wasting nearly a quarter of the slide — and where a distinctive background is genuinely wanted, use an airbrushed blend of two related dark colours behind light type.

Fix the background colour before the rest of the palette, choosing dark or light from the formality of the event and the venue size, because pure black and pure white afford the greatest contrast while mid-range coloured backgrounds render parts of a palette unusable.

Trade off dark against light backgrounds on their known consequences: dark reads formal, suits large venues, lets objects glow, and fails as a handout; light reads informal, illuminates the room, prints well, suits small rooms, and forgoes dramatic lighting.

Use animation to control the order in which a slide is taken in: hold back a second visual element until the first has been explained, and reveal a complicated visual piecemeal so the audience follows one connection at a time — but never start from an empty body, since some visual evidence should be present for the slide's whole projection.

Keep the balance between saying and showing, because when most of the speaker's sentences are already readable on the slide many listeners stop listening — and a deck in which most slides carry no image serves little purpose beyond supplying sentences to read.

Guide the audience's eyes through every slide explicitly — for text, diagrams, and images alike — and when the required flow runs counter to natural eye movement, either build the graphic in the intended order over time or mark the starting point with a clear symbol or arrow.
Make animation look natural and alive with familiar movement that conveys interrelatedness or sequence and lets the audience process information in the order presented.

Pan between scenes rather than piling content onto one slide: split the content and join the slides with a push transition so the audience perceives one continuous space, since content shown all at once is illegible and drives them to read ahead.
Keep every text block to one or two lines, because focus groups found nearly everyone reads a block of that length while more than half will not read a block of three lines or longer.
Arrange images so the order to view them is unmistakable, following the audience's reading direction or enforcing it by animation or layering, and credit every source while observing copyright.
Own every image in the deck and never take one from the Web, because a presentation that spreads online exposes the author to expensive usage claims from the rights holder.

Design a diagram carrying equations or code so the audience need only recognise those blocks as equations or code rather than decipher them, since such a diagram can be assembled by simple copying and arrangement without professional artwork.

Walk an audience through a graph methodically — the y-axis, the x-axis, and what each curve represents — before animating in the marking that highlights the assertion, and slow down for complicated visual evidence, because the speaker has lived with the graph for months while the audience is seeing it for the first time and needs soak time.
Keep the eyes on the audience while speaking, the one legitimate exception being the explanation of a graphic, equation, or film the audience is already looking at.

Design quantitative material to lead the audience on a journey of discovery rather than sifting data and passing it on, and consider animating a static relationship over time to surface an insight the still figure hides.

Make every line in the visual evidence contribute as every word in the headline does: remove the default outer box a graphing program draws around a plot, and add a border only where it separates a photograph or rectangular drawing from the background rather than uniformly.
