Prefer either a succinct assertion headline or no headline at all to a topic phrase, which does not convey enough to justify the space it consumes; omitting the headline frees space to enlarge the graphic at the cost that the spoken words alone must then carry the message.

Build the visual aids only after the story is settled, tightening each drafted assertion into a headline readable during the talk and creating graphics purpose-made for projection rather than reusing a paper's figures, which usually carry too much detail or lettering too small to work.

Use the plain Appear transition as the default and reserve decorative schemes such as Fly In, Bounce, Swivel, Pulse, Teeter, and Spin for the case where actual physical movement in the science is being shown, since they otherwise distract, annoy, and undercut the talk's professionalism.

Hold a projected table to the two-to-four rule on both rows and columns, since too many cells shrink the text below readability and leave the audience unsure where to look — an effect a laser pointer cannot repair — and bring sections in by animation or emphasise them with colour.

Replace a bulleted list with the visual form of the relationship it actually holds — a timeline for chronological details, call-outs around an image for spatial ones, a pie graph for relative sizes, and a diagram for a flow — because the list presents details without showing how they connect and leaves the audience to work the relation out.
Convert a bullet slide into a picture by circling its verbs or nouns and naming the relationship they form, which usually falls into a known category of visual relationship.

Treat displayed data as a diagram chosen by intended reading — comparison, trend over time, or distribution — and prefer designs that carry multiple parameters into a richer cause-and-effect story over ones that oversimplify the statistics.
Anchor tabular data to a map where the data is geographically indexed and reveal it sequentially, which makes the locations memorable and keeps the audience on the part under discussion.

Size type so that everyone in the room can read the headline and the body — 10 and 12 point are legible only in the first few rows — because failing to spend the time to make a slide readable is inconsiderate to the audience.

Validate minimum type size empirically rather than by rule — the tape-at-N-feet-for-an-N-inch-screen test, slide sorter at 66 percent, clicking through from the venue's back row, or the oldest audience member's age halved — and treat 28 point as the keynote floor, since dropping under 24 point with third-level bullets means a document has been built.

Force a large minimum type size, because small type comes from not knowing the material well enough or believing more text is more convincing, while the size floor compels the presenter to find and explain the most salient points.

Put a short reference listing — often just an author surname and a year — on every slide carrying a photograph, drawing, or graph from someone else's work: not everyone need be able to read it, but everyone must see that it exists, because failing to acknowledge another group's contribution is at minimum an insult and is more typically regarded as theft.

Never set slide text in all capitals: readers identify words partly by the shape of ascenders and descenders, which capitals erase, forcing every letter to be read — and capitals consume about 35 percent more space that would be better left blank.
Test the colour combination on a projected screen before the talk, because a contrast that looks adequate on the author's monitor can be entirely unreadable when projected.

Verify the palette by projection, not on the authoring screen: check contrast against the background and among the chosen colours, tweak manually while projecting, and either bring your own projector or arrive early enough to adjust the venue's.

Choose a high-contrast combination and avoid the mid-tones that are neither dark enough to contrast with white type nor light enough to contrast with black: black on yellow reads fastest and black on white next, black on red and red on black are among the slowest, and dark blue or dark green on white is fast enough to serve.

Pick the background by talk length, room conditions, and downstream use: white suits shorter talks and imports of equations and graphs that arrive on white, a darker background is softer over a long talk, but an aged bulb, a bright room, or an audience likely to print the deck all argue for white.

Avoid the red, green, and brown combinations that colour blindness makes indistinguishable — both for type against background and as more than one curve colour on a single graph — since a significant share of any audience is affected at rates varying by gender and ancestry.

Account for colour's emotional effect independently of its contrast — blue and green read as soothing to Western audiences while orange, red, and even yellow backgrounds agitate — and treat the institution's identifying colours as secondary to both contrast and that effect.

Choose colour as a deliberate signal of tone and expectation, screened against three questions: does it appeal to this audience, does it differentiate from competitors while avoiding colours that read negatively in this industry, and does it reflect who the presenter or organization is.
Never give every colour equal value: keep added colours subordinate to the core palette to avoid overwhelming the audience, adding black sparingly where contrast must carry emphasis.

Keep logos secondary: show the institution's logo at some point and on any distributed slide, but on projected slides only the first and last need it, place it in a bottom corner rather than the upper-left real estate the assertion headline claims, and remove any logo that crowds the visual evidence.
Drop the per-slide logo in favour of identifying the presenter on the first and last bumper slides, and if a logo on every slide is mandated, place it in the lower right where text can rag around it.

Open blank space between a slide's elements, since too little does three separate kinds of damage — the slide feels crowded, the viewing order becomes ambiguous, and the audience bounces inefficiently between elements — and the default master causes it by reserving obsolete transparency-era gutters and by setting text larger than it needs to be.
Check slide format on whether the type is easy to read, blank space used effectively, weak software defaults avoided, the slide left room to breathe, and any animation purposeful and professional.
Prefer clean minimalist slide design over the cluttered data-dense default common in technical presentations.
Master slide design across three fronts — arrangement, visual elements, and movement — and treat the slide as a signal that either delivers information or becomes noise the viewer tunes out.
Force a priority decision on every slide — give some elements dominance and restrain others — because putting everything on one slide at equal value is laziness and overcrowding adds no clarity.

Treat whitespace as a first-class slide element whose use or misuse largely determines effectiveness, and read any slide that sacrifices whitespace for content as packed too tightly — at which point the slide is the wrong tool for that content.

Reduce an overloaded slide by asking what can be removed without changing the meaning and where the content can be split, because a slide's value is the clarity of its message, not the amount of information it holds — clear space is fine and clutter is a design failure.

Make the title slide orient rather than announce: relevant images give the speaker several possible entry points — scope, importance, or history — into the same talk for different audiences, where the default title-names-institutions slide turns the opening into a hurried obligation and leaves the audience disoriented the moment it changes.

Reject persistent-navigation templates that list every topic on every slide, which spend 10 to 20 percent or more of the most valuable space on a job an effective mapping slide plus spoken transitions already does; the cheaper cue for a long talk is a small icon from the mapping slide in a bottom corner, under 5 percent of the slide and able to replace the logo.

Do not use clip art, which reads as unprofessional and undercuts the seriousness of the topic; a real photograph, even of the blackboard on which a model was derived, carries a far more professional tone.

Borrow individual TED strategies, such as letting a photograph bleed off the page, into otherwise conventional assertion-evidence slides when the time or artistic skill for the full approach is unavailable.

Use pecha kucha — 20 slides at 20 seconds each on automatic advance — where there is no time to teach a sophisticated structure, since the rigid window forces presenters off bullet-ridden slides onto visual ones, accepting that it demands substantial preparation to compress each scene's speech and that some scenes such as a graph do not fit.

Reserve the Lessig style — short phrases and images flashed for about a second each in synch with the speech — for keynotes and after-dinner talks delivered on multiple occasions, because audiences perceive it as light-hearted and one 15-minute talk can run to more than 300 slides requiring continual practice to hold the timing.

Match the sequencing strategy to the situation: evidence-assertion for teaching or for complex and controversial assertions, pecha kucha where a sophisticated structure cannot be taught, Lessig for keynotes and after-dinner talks, and Prezi for zooming through a large system or timeline.

Practise until the talk can be given with no notes by memorising its organisation — the test being that the speaker knows the next slide before advancing to it — and consider speaking the next slide's assertion aloud just before advancing so that listeners who grasp it turn straight to the visual evidence while the projected headline catches the rest.

Control digression with in-talk benchmarks — finishing the introduction or reaching the second main point by a set time, checked with a glance at a watch or room clock while changing slides — and make them actionable by building in an optional point to cover if on time and skip if behind.

Reduce each slide until the audience can process it in under three seconds — keep only elements that aid recall, cut phrases to single words — and move the remaining detail into the notes, which can hold unlimited material and can be run as a presenter-view teleprompter.
Design every slide as a visual aid that reinforces what the presenter says, never as text for the audience to read, because an audience listens or reads but cannot do both.
Give the presenter structure without a script: slides should scaffold the talk rather than put words in the presenter's mouth, because a detailed script blocks connection with the audience.

Diagnose the presenter's relationship to their slides as codependent, interdependent, or independent, because dense default-template slides turn into a teleprompter that replaces rehearsal and connection with reading aloud.

Use Prezi's zoomable single canvas for explaining a whole system divided into parts — a timeline, a diagram, or a map — accepting that it costs more learning time and forbids animating details into a focused scene, and staying with zooming rather than the twisting and rotating transitions that physically unsettle audiences.

Build a complex visual up over time rather than exposing it whole — a system diagram assembled from several diagram types, or a chart drawn and revealed progressively while speaking — because the audience can only process one idea at a time.

Plan on the assumption that whatever can go wrong will go wrong at the worst possible time: projection failures come in a predictable set — no image, no sound, no internet for a film, a software mismatch, a resolution mismatch — and it is roughly even odds that something is amiss at the start.

Never attempt a live demonstration without rehearsal, since an unpractised one can injure the presenter and hijack the lesson, and a demonstration failure at the culminating moment of a bid can cost the contract outright.

Rehearse with the actual equipment, since rehearsal exposes both the pitfalls that would startle the presenter mid-performance and the device-specific traps that strike at the start — and while rehearsal guarantees nothing, since practised demonstrations still fail, it greatly increases the odds.

Remove the dependencies that fail in an unfamiliar room: embed every image and film in a local file with a backup on separate media rather than relying on internet access many organisations restrict, keep a teleconferenced presentation simple because films lock up and sound clips feed back in transmission, and bring one's own laptop where the deck needs unusual typefaces, settings, formats, or films.

Imagine the worst compound case once the structure and slides are set and devise a plan for equipment failure, since disasters arise from chains of causes rather than single ones; where the equipment is unproven, design the talk so it can be delivered from handouts alone, and carry a troubleshooting kit of video and audio cables and a small computer-powered speaker plus the knowledge of how to match the laptop's resolution to the projector.

Decide whether to include a visual aid on three factors — the complexity of the demonstration or equipment, the gain if it succeeds, and the loss if it fails — proceeding only when the benefit outweighs the risk and always planning a response to failure.

Arrive early enough that a failure is recoverable — ten minutes of margin is enough to discover a missing typeface, substitute one, and refit the text boxes before the audience sees anything — because presenters who arrive as the session starts subject a large audience to one of the most painful scenes in scientific presentation.

Never deliver an entire scheduled presentation impromptu: the odds of an efficient structure with proper emphasis and smooth transitions are low, the potential to become lost is high, there is little scope for visual aids, and the prospect of becoming lost is itself a deep source of nervousness whose best countermeasure is preparation.
Typeset presentation text properly rather than treating it as beneath the effort, because most people recognize when type is balanced and typographic laziness distracts a share of any audience.

Expect at least one occasion where everything fails despite rehearsal, early arrival, and anticipation, and respond by keeping one's cool, retaining control of the proceedings, and where possible turning the apparent failure to advantage.

Meet a caustic question with a calm but resolute voice and work methodically through several perspectives on the concern raised, since keeping cool demonstrates that the speaker rather than the questioner controls the presentation and multiple perspectives refuse the either-or trap such questioners lay.

Seize control when a questioner rambles, because the audience's irritation transfers from the questioner to the passive speaker and undermines an otherwise worthwhile presentation — a strong presentation being two-way communication in which the speaker also carries the responsibility to learn from the audience and adjust.

Account for how full the room is as much as how large it is, since a filled room amplifies a laugh while in a half-filled one the same laughter dissipates — and where discussion among the audience is the goal, a U-shaped seating arrangement beats rows because listeners can meet each other's eyes.

Do not try to orchestrate every element of delivery at once, since attending consciously to posture, gesture, expression, eye contact, volume, variation, and filler words at the same time leaves the speaker stiff and self-conscious while neglecting bigger things such as genuine enthusiasm.

Study other speakers' delivery with a critical eye, and shortly before going on stage imagine a model speaker delivering the talk — their vocal rhythm and movement — since this whole-motion method borrowed from sport draws out the traits the speaker values rather than diminishing their individuality.

Check delivery on whether the speaker showed passion, made effective eye contact, controlled nervousness, moved in ways that contribute, exuded confidence, handled the equipment properly, kept the voice clear and engaging at an appropriate speed, avoided filler phrases, handled questions convincingly and succinctly, and kept to time.

Deploy structural, delivery and emotional contrast together rather than relying on one, as a strong talk states the gap explicitly, alternates modes of delivery, and moves the audience between laughter and feeling.

Convey interest in the subject, since the most captivating technical speakers are those who love their subjects and know them well and a speaker who conveys none cannot expect the audience to feel any — shown through a sincere voice, sustained eye contact, animated expressions, and natural gestures rather than through singing and shouting, which reads as pretence.
Hold back the dazzle, especially at the opening, because scientific audiences read a highly polished delivery as a sign the talk is more style than substance.
Reserve a quiet block alone immediately before a talk — accomplished speakers take at least thirty minutes even on a tenth delivery, and skipping it is treated as disrespectful to the audience.

Use silence deliberately: pause at least a couple of times long enough to hear the room's ventilation hum, which gives the speaker emphasis and the audience reflection, and a speaker who values silence stops wasting it on fillers.

Accept that mistakes will happen when working in a second language, since embarrassment leads to avoiding speech and improvement is impossible without speaking; writing out entire presentations and rehearsing them repeatedly is a legitimate compensation.

Choose the source of words deliberately from four options with known trade-offs — extemporaneous buys earned credibility, easy adjustment, eye contact, and a natural pace at the cost of inexact wording and much preparation, while reading buys precision and smoothness at the cost of pace, eye contact, adaptability, and credibility.

Match the source of words to the occasion: extemporaneous for conference talks, business meetings, seminars, and lectures; impromptu for answering and asking questions and for roundtable discussion; memorisation for the first or last sentences, a short quotation, or a brief introduction of another speaker; and reading for a press conference, a quotation, a scrutinised management talk, or an emotional speech such as a eulogy.

Default to a practised extemporaneous talk for most scientific presentations — a rehearsed talk following an established organisation held in memory, in notes, or in the visual aids — because a meticulously memorised speech collapses the moment the audience opens on the offensive and forces improvisation.

Keep notes out of view and glance at them silently rather than holding cards in the hand, because a visible card distracts and undermines the speaker's authority before an audience that expects them to look people in the eye and speak from what they know.
Put the notes on the presenter's own screen as the comfort monitor while the audience sees only the image, rather than using the projected screen as a teleprompter.

Expect extemporaneous speech to align the speaker's pace with the audience's comprehension automatically, since the words come less easily on a difficult idea — exactly where the audience needs more time — and to leave the eyes free to read the audience and adjust when listeners look confused or bored.

Eliminate filler phrases by first learning which ones you actually use, typically from a colleague's critique — after which catching yourself saying one means the habit is already breaking — and get a full night's sleep before an important talk, since fillers surface far more when a speaker is tired.

Memorise only short high-stakes fragments — introducing a colleague, or the first couple of sentences of a difficult talk — which secures a good first impression and gets the words flowing to the point where concentration shifts to the science and the opening nervousness disappears.

Keep memorising the actual words the exception even among heavy preparers — justified mainly by an unusually compressed slot — while the standard remains a practised but extemporaneous talk, and aim for the confidence that rests on knowing the subject, loving it, genuinely enjoying explaining it, and having prepared with that passion fuelling the preparation.

Treat reading a speech as costly by default: it runs too fast for comprehension, puts the speaker's eyes on the page so neither party can read the other, and above all leaves the audience wondering whether the speaker knows the subject — a penalty that is real in science and engineering even where other disciplines have a tradition of reading papers aloud.
Stay connected to the four things around the presentation — the room, oneself, the audience, and the time — rather than carrying oneself as though disconnected from all of them.

Shift focus off oneself and onto the listeners — meeting them beforehand and asking them questions — because the speaker is working for the audience and residual nervous energy then works for the presentation.
Move company and presenter background out of the opening and into a handout so the presentation itself can begin at the audience's frequency; relocate the information rather than dropping it.
The audience crosses the threshold by conscious choice and cannot be forced, so the presentation's objective is to bring them to that decision well enough that they cross voluntarily.
Prepare the audience for the journey they will undertake after leaving the room, and exploit the fact that a presentation is not bound to chronological order when addressing those later stages.

Define the presentation's destination — where the audience should be when they leave — before building content, and require every piece of content to propel them toward it, because an unmapped audience does not arrive.
Resonance causes change, and an audience will persist in a state of rest unless compelled to change — so a presentation that produces no movement has not resonated.

Aim for the presence of an individual conversation with each audience member, and get it from preparation — internalized content, settled staging, and rehearsal — rather than from stage presence alone.

Match the medium to the room and the audience rather than defaulting to projection: projection suits a big room and a big audience, while projecting for a couple of people reads as impersonal, and flip charts or flip books suit small collaborative settings where the audience enjoys watching someone draw.

Aim for interdependence with the slides in a three-party relationship that includes the audience, so the media lets the audience see what the presenter is saying instead of showcasing the presenter or their crutches.
Show a new audience early that the talk will deliver, because so many of their past experiences have been empty ones that they arrive fearing the worst.

Take charge of the room as part of delivery — bringing a remote advancer if you intend to walk, moving furniture that blocks the walking space, and adjusting lights or shades — because passive presenters end up on the wrong side of the screen or projecting washed-out slides, and the speaker is the one credited or blamed for the result.

Arrive early to a shared session, learn the setup, and work with it rather than against it, since arriving at the last minute and demanding different equipment can wreck the following speaker's talk as well as one's own.

Use attire deliberately, since it influences the perceived formality of the occasion and a professional appearance gives a new audience a good first impression — while recognising that appropriate attire is not always formal and a deliberately casual look can be right when it positions the speaker as the outsider.

Vary loudness and speed to engage the audience and emphasise key details, since a voice with no variation tires them quickly — but keep the variation within the speaker's natural conversational inflection, because an audience senses when a speaker is acting; pitch and accent are not worth trying to change.

Adopt a stance that is both confident and comfortable — hands relaxed at the side or rested lightly on a podium rather than clenching it — keeping a hand out of a pocket at the opening and still thereafter, and emptying keys and change beforehand.
Do not let lists of forbidden postures inhibit a speaker's energy: an accomplished lecturer may adopt several of them provided the audience is already engaged and the posture is held only briefly.

Move with purpose so the movement contributes — walking toward the audience to emphasise a point, using the hands to illustrate so the audience sees as well as hears — and watch for the repetitive movements that hypnotise: fidgeting with a tie, necklace, or belt, shifting weight, or pacing.

Channel nervous energy into the talk rather than merely surviving it, since unchannelled energy escapes as jingling coins, a fiddled pointer, or swaying in place — and scrunching the toes gives it an outlet the audience cannot see.

Prefer a long physical pointer, which keeps the speaker out of the projector beam and can be grounded against the screen; where a laser pointer is used, anchor it against the side because it amplifies a nervous hand into a wild vibration, watch where it is aimed, and use it sparingly since highlighting nearly everything provides no emphasis.

Direct the audience's attention with the eyes, since they follow the speaker's gaze to the floor, the window, or back to themselves; the workable rule is to have met everyone's eyes before the end in a small room and to have looked several times at every section in a large one, while the advice to look above their heads at the back wall is a myth that teaches the speaker nothing.
Guide the audience through whichever structure is chosen with clear verbal or visual cues stating where the presenter is and where the audience is being taken.

Read the audience continuously — intent stares signal concentration, nodding agreement, closed eyes or a gaze at the floor that concentration has stopped, and faces reveal delight, confusion, anger, or boredom — and adjust by slowing when they look confused, speeding up when bored, and cutting tangential points when tired.

Read the whole room's mood but never overreact to one individual: an angry face may have nothing to do with the talk and is best not looked at directly, and a listener determined to sleep should be left to sleep.

Treat the allotted time as a hard commitment, since a speaker who ignores the chair's signals and speaks through the break is remembered for that rather than for the work — and recognise that without interruptions the speaker owns the clock while in an interactive format it is shared with the audience.
Plan one or two invisible slide jumps by typing the target slide number and pressing Enter, keeping those numbers — plus any wanted during the question period — on a sticky note beside the laptop.

Decide whether to yield to a persistent questioner by standing and shared interest: a manager or funder usually has to be given their time and a tangent several listeners want may be worth deferring to, but when one person alone is holding up everyone else, move on — because the audience's irritation at that questioner turns into anger at the speaker who let the talk derail.

Treat pre-talk nervousness as normal and shared even by great scientists, requiring only that it not pull the presentation down — the visible failure being the zombie state in which the face loses expression and the voice loses energy.

Watch for nervousness in the voice, where it appears as a shake lasting minutes, as a loss of nerve that reduces the talk to a dull unintelligible reading, or as an acceleration that finishes a 50-minute talk in 30.

Take comfort in the predictable cycle of nervousness, which subsides as soon as the presentation begins and the speaker concentrates on the subject, and reframe the moment by remembering that most of the audience is resigned to yet another boring presentation — which turns the talk into a challenge in the positive sense.

Use the athletic toolkit against nerves: visualise delivering a successful talk and stating each main assertion with the audience nodding, breathe deeply and quietly so the body can counteract the chemistry of nervousness, and tighten and release the muscles progressively from the feet upward while waiting to be called.

Hold composure through anything mid-talk, since an alarming event may have nothing to do with the talk and audiences do not hold a speaker responsible for failed bulbs, fire alarms, or other listeners' behaviour — only for how the speaker reacts; even devastating criticism immediately before speaking leaves one correct move, which is to go up and do the best possible with the cards dealt.

Handle a question through an ordered sequence: listen to it, ask for clarification if it is unclear — legitimate rather than embarrassing since it was fashioned on the spot — repeat or rephrase it when the room is too large for others to have heard, pause to think, and only then answer, balancing satisfying the questioner against staying concise enough that others still get a chance.

Avoid filler phrases in any response to a hostile question, since stumbling into them makes the speaker appear weak and confused, and consider the decisive alternative of pausing, fixing the eyes on the questioner, answering, and immediately calling on someone in a different part of the room so no follow-up is possible.

Never bluff an in-scope answer, since exposure is likely and credibility collapses when it comes; the honest replies are to admit the answer is incomplete and state what is known, to say nobody yet knows if that is true — which can win respect and shows command of the literature — or to promise to look it up afterwards and then actually do so.

Read a challenge from the floor as usually not a personal attack, since eminent scientists rigorously challenged work they believed inaccurate and such challenges often strengthen the science — but answer strongly when the challenge is to the work's assumptions, because an audience that comes to regard those as flawed discounts the entire result.

Meet a challenge with one of three tested responses: stand straight and answer loudly enough for the whole room even if only restating the formal point; distinguish sincere questions from attacks, answering the first politely and rebutting the second directly with the pertinent literature, calmly enumerating the papers that support a challenged assumption; or lower the voice rather than raise it to guide the audience's sympathy, which works as long as the speaker stays resolute.

Replace the question of how to handle nervousness with the question of how to achieve confidence, whose answer is passion combined with preparation — passion alone being only a source of it — supported in the moment by focusing on the science rather than on the audience.

Calibrate preparation against what confident speakers actually do — rehearsing the opening 10 to 15 times, or practising an 18-minute talk two or three times a day for the two months before it — which is far above what most presenters assume.

Plan several deliberate delivery-mode changes within an hour — alternate media, multiple presenters, interaction, movement, a dramatic gesture — because media-conditioned audiences begin to squirm within about ten minutes of an unvaried speaker, and the key to holding attention is having something new happen continually.

Scale preparation time to the stakes and schedule it: book preparation and review cycles as soon as the engagement is known, treat roughly 36 to 90 hours as the range for an hour-long 30-slide talk, and reserve from-scratch development for the high-stakes cases while allowing minimal reuse for low-stakes ones.

Check the middle on whether the assertions were emphasised and supported, the needed information conveyed with terms defined and background given, and the emphasis appropriate; check scope and depth as three separate questions — whether the scope engages, the key limitations were stated, and the depth satisfies.

Check transitions at three junctures — beginning to middle, between the main points of the middle, and middle to ending — and check the ending on whether the main assertions were summarised, closure achieved, repetition and placement used effectively for emphasis, and sources acknowledged.
Tune the message to the audience's existing beliefs and desires rather than expecting the audience to tune itself to the presenter; build the message from what is already inside them.
Adopt humility as the operating stance, because audience insight and resonance are only available to a presenter who holds it.

Treat disagreement between presenter and audience as a resource rather than a problem: oppositional content is stimulating and familiar content comforting, and their polarity is what produces forward movement, so know the audience well enough to state where the views are alike and where they differ.
Never frame the audience as helping the presenter on their journey; an audience can always spot selfish motives, so any benefit to the presenter must remain secondary.

Map the overlap between presenter and audience deliberately, since establishing what is shared simultaneously identifies what lies outside it — precisely the material the audience must be brought to embrace.

Inoculate against objections by stating the opposing points inside the talk before the audience can raise them, which demonstrates the presenter has thought everything through and lowers their anxiety.

Give the material an explicit structure, because without one ideas are forgotten, audiences expect structure, and dumping unstructured information signals the presenter does not know what to do with what they gathered.

Plant a handful of succinct, repeatable sound bites so the audience can recall and transfer the message, coordinating key phrases word-for-word with the press release and preparing at least one fifteen- to thirty-second message salient enough that a reporter will obviously feature it.
Treat each audience member as a broadcast node with their own following, so key concepts must be crisp enough to be repeated verbatim and forwarded far beyond the room.

Treat the presentation as a signal passing through sender, transmission, reception and receiver, where distortion can enter at any step; minimize credibility, semantic, experiential and bias noise at every stage through careful planning and rehearsing, because each step either strengthens the signal or adds noise that makes the audience tune out.
Make the similarities and differences between presenter and audience clear early so they get through sizing the presenter up quickly and a common identity is established.

Use slides as stage setting rather than the message, because the presenter delivers the message and an audience processes only one inbound stream at a time — they will either listen or read, never both.

Be transparent so the audience can see past the presenter to the idea, which requires three things: be honest — sharing failures and how they were overcome rather than posing as flawless; be unique — surfacing the differences that bring new insight instead of concealing them to fit in; and do not compromise — speaking confidently and accepting that ridicule or rejection is sometimes the price.

Build the presentation around what the audience needs and will do rather than around the presenter's agenda: they came to find out what the presenter can do for them, so give them a reason for their time, content that resonates, clarity about what to do next, and use their needs as the benchmark for checking the message.

Think like a designer when presenting: make every decision intentional, let reason and logic drive placement, let meaning drive order and hierarchy, and accept that these decisions feed the audience's perception of who the presenter is.
Shape a presentation as a contour with multiple peaks rather than a dramatic story's single climax, because a presentation carries layered and disparate information rather than one protagonist's arc.
Give the presentation a clear beginning, middle and end with an identifiable structure, an opening turning point that captures intrigue, and a beginning and end much shorter than the middle.

Treat these story models as forms rather than formulas — they fix structure and transformation while leaving room for creativity — and note that the screenplay paradigm is only partially applicable to presentations.
Put the presentation into story form to obtain three properties at once: structure, an imbalance the audience wants resolved, and a clearly identified gap the audience can fill.
Creating contrast does not require rebelling against the organization's existing messages; the requirement is to lift that content out of its drab traditional treatment.

Pair facts with emotional appeal rather than choosing between them: use plenty of evidence but accompany it with appeals to desire, since logical agreement alone does not produce action and stacking more proof does not convert a determined skeptic.

Include logical appeal in every presentation without exception — a structure that holds the talk together, a stated claim, and evidence supporting it — and build ethical appeal from shared values plus the right analytical-emotional balance.
Before designing emotional appeals, be able to name the audience's emotions, describe their causes and know how they are aroused.

Build the middle from contrast that visibly moves up and down so the audience feels events continually unfolding, drawing on three distinct kinds: content contrast between what is and what could be, emotional contrast between analytical and emotional material, and delivery contrast between traditional and nontraditional methods.
Engineer one emotional peak in which the audience personally experiences what the presenter has been explaining, placed after they have been equipped to perceive it.

Build empathy by answering concrete questions about the audience — what makes them laugh, cry, what unites them, what incites them, what makes them deserve to win — rather than cataloguing attributes abstractly.
Balance analytical and emotional appeal appropriately rather than maximizing emotion; emotional appeal receives emphasis because it is underused, not because it outranks analysis.

Let the topic set the natural weighting — emotionally charged subjects invite emotional argument while science, engineering, finance and academia invite analytical ones — but never leave an analytically weighted presentation void of emotion.
Use story as the working mechanism for emotional engagement, because a story binds information to experience and makes static information dynamic in a way a well-formed argument does not.
Incorporating story into presentations has an outsized effect on outcomes, and knowing the audience's resonant frequency and tuning to it is what makes them move.
Prefer the personal story whose conflict or complication exposes the presenter's own flaws, since that is the story with the most power to change others even though telling it requires vulnerability.
Sprinkle personal stories of risk, frailty and victory — including ones where the presenter was corrected — because they make the presenter credible and transparent.
Strip jargon and emotionally neutral corporate phrasing, because they are the easy default but block the human connection an audience attends an in-person presentation to get.

Treat the audience as a line of individuals awaiting a face-to-face conversation rather than a homogeneous blob, since that framing produces the conversational tone that keeps people engaged even though each listener filters the same message differently.

Frame every pre-presentation communication — the invitation, agenda, email wording and speaker bio — as part of the first impression, and use the time in the room beforehand to greet and question attendees, because arriving harried signals distraction and sets a cold tone before a word is spoken.

Never assume the audience has kept up with the presenter's field: specialized jargon aimed at nonspecialists reduces the help and funding an idea attracts purely because listeners do not understand it, and this applies inside one organization where departments trade in different languages and acronyms.

Cast the audience as the hero and the presenter as the mentor: defer to them, make each member feel addressed personally, and judge success by what they leave holding rather than by how impressive the presenter appeared.

Discharge the mentor's two duties — teaching and gift-giving — by supplying important, useful, previously unknown information plus guidance, confidence and tools, so the audience leaves knowing something new they can apply.

Build common ground from shared experiences and shared goals, and reveal qualifications humbly as evidence of a similar journey completed, because audiences validate a presenter against their own criteria before adopting a new perspective and commonalities are what bolster credibility.

Distinguish a report from a presentation and route each to its own medium: reports organize facts by topic and should be distributed, presentations organize scenes dramatically and should be presented, and projecting a document as a read-along produces neither.

When the content really is a document, change the format rather than the slides: hold a meeting, circulate the document beforehand or let the audience read it at the start, and spend the rest of the time on discussion and action plans — and if the goal is only to convey facts and figures, cancel the meeting and send a report.
Distribute the data as a printout instead of projecting it whenever the audience must examine it and reach their own conclusions, because slides are a poor medium for complex data.
Layer fact and story alternately through the talk, because the alternation creates a pulse and makes the information more digestible than either alone.

Recast information in anecdotal form, since a story charges the information emotionally, makes it digestible and makes it easy for the audience to repeat, and may run from one sentence to a theme threaded through the whole talk.
Shift the goal from transferring information to creating an experience, which is done by creating desire in the audience and then showing how the idea fills it.

In organizations, communicating each strategic move persuasively is part of the survival process, and a future direction may have to be argued without supporting statistics because the data does not yet exist.
Put something at stake that convinces the audience a great deal will be lost if the goal is not reached, because material with nothing at risk is not interesting.
Hand the audience a usable tool that removes the specific barrier keeping them from valuing the idea, teaching them to perceive what they previously could not.
A big idea without a compelling statement of what is at stake falls flat, because the stakes are what let the audience recognize the need to participate.
Invest care in communicating an idea in proportion to the value placed on it, because an idea that is not communicated well loses its value and adds nothing.
Build on the universal story pattern of situation, complication and resolution, where resolution means a solution rather than merely an ending.

Use the Hero's Journey to map the audience's passage from their ordinary world into the presenter's special world, where they gain insight and skills to bring back, remembering that the hero's outer journey is accompanied by an inner transformation at each stage.
Target perception first, because the audience must change internally before they will change how they act.

Design the first impression deliberately across everything the audience encounters — room, lighting, music, items on chairs, the image on screen, clothing and entrance — because within seconds the audience classifies the presenter and judges whether they can connect.

Create the imbalance that makes an audience care by deliberately juxtaposing what is with what could be — contrasting who they are entering the room with who they could be leaving it — since a perceived gap is what forces them to contend with the discord until a new balance is reached.

Identify and align with values the audience already holds, because they choose whether to connect, will usually respond only when it serves their interest, and their personal values ultimately drive behaviour.

Make the call to adventure an explicit, memorable big idea conveying what could be, delivered at the moment the audience first sees the stark contrast with what is; the turning point must not be muddled or vague, and everything after it exists to fill that gap.

State exactly what the audience must do as discrete, simple, easily executed tasks with the most critical ones emphasized, each connectable by the audience to a positive outcome for themselves or the greater good.

Offer at least one action suited to each of the four audience temperaments — doers who instigate activities, suppliers who bring resources, influencers who change perceptions, and innovators who generate ideas — so every member can choose the contribution they are comfortable making.

Profile the audience along six dimensions — lifestyle, existing knowledge and biases, motivation and desire, values, influences and how they decide, and how they give and receive respect — and look specifically for how the idea would relieve pressure on their real circumstances.
Never end on the call to action: follow the to-do list with a vivid picture of the reward, since ending on tasks is not inspirational.

Land the ending on a higher plane than the beginning: repeat the most important points, then describe with wonder and awe the world that exists once the idea is adopted, showing the reward is worth the effort and asserting the idea is not merely possible but the right and better choice.

Load the closing material with the inspirational payload, because by the principle of recency audiences remember the last content most vividly and a rousing conclusion produces emotional contagion and a strong takeaway.
Never over-amplify emotion: an audience that feels manipulated is lost, emotional appeal is only effective when it furthers the argument, and imbalance in either direction damages credibility.
Treat adoption as undecided when the talk ends: the audience determines the outcome, so plan what happens after the room empties rather than counting delivery as completion.

Diagnose a presentation by charting its contour as a sparkline — the line moving between what is and what could be, coloured for emotional and delivery contrast — so weak stretches become visible before delivery.
Follow the presentation form flexibly rather than rigidly, because rigid adherence makes presentations predictable and the form's versatility is part of its value.
Never design a presentation without a specific audience in mind; doing so is like addressing a love letter to whom it may concern.
End every presentation with a clear call to action that answers 'so what?', and plan explicitly for how the audience might resist adopting it.

Treat design as problem solving and experience rather than decoration, while recognizing that dressing up a presentation is not itself a business benefit even though design-oriented firms have outperformed their peers.
Narrowly targeting the message at the highest-priority individuals so it reads as a personal conversation is legitimate, and is worthwhile even if only that one right person acts.

Do not stop at demographics: workplace, title, geography and company yield only assumptions, so research the audience actively through surveys, their industry's blogs and icons, their social conversation, press releases, annual reports and their own presentations until they feel known personally.

Let the occasion dictate the segmentation: where circumstances create a natural situational grouping, address each subaudience in turn and bind them back to the collective whole rather than defaulting to conventional demographic or political distinctions.
Move credibly between speaker roles when different audience segments require different things from the same address.

Establish the audience's likability to yourself before writing content, and keep asking about them until the picture shifts from what they do for a job to who they are, since liking them is the precondition for being genuine and titles alone are not enough.
The objective of audience analysis is to determine what the audience cares about and to link the idea to it in the most relevant and believable way available.
Common ground can unite an otherwise diverse group toward a shared purpose, because people set aside differences when strongly connected to a common goal.
Expect the audience to feel a sense of loss as they move away from their familiar world, since persuasion asks them to let go of old beliefs or habits before adopting new ones.

Harness resistance rather than trying to eliminate it: the severity cannot be controlled, but adjusting the message to the opposing force produces forward progress, which requires tacking back and forth rather than driving straight ahead.

Write the big idea — the single controlling message — as a complete sentence that articulates the presenter's unique point of view and conveys what is at stake; a topic is not a big idea, and using the word "you" is better still because it ensures the idea is addressed to someone.
Work the two emotional levers deliberately: raise the likelihood of pain and lower pleasure for rejecting the big idea, or raise pleasure and lower pain for accepting it.

Ground a change message in a hard look at the organization's competitive situation, market position, technological trends and financial performance, then communicate that broadly and dramatically around timely crises, potential crises or opportunities.

Structure a change message as a repeated matrix of move-from-being, move-to-doing, benefit or outcome, and a personalized story, reinforcing it with contrasting words and images and carrying the contrast into the title itself.
Match the gravity of the presentation to the severity of the actual situation and reflect what is at stake accurately — no more and no less — so urgency is neither inflated nor understated.

Plan the audience's arc the way a story analyst reads a screenplay's first and last page: specify where they start and where they end, name both the inward and the outward transformation, and treat the outward change as the observable proof the big idea was believed.

Alternatively define the journey by process segmentation: locate the phase most of the audience occupies in a project process, sales cycle or adoption curve and build messages to move them to the next phase.

Name the sacrifice the request demands, because adopting a new perspective always costs something — at minimum abandoning what was previously held true — and even a request for the audience's time takes an irretrievable slice of their lives.

Enumerate the audience's sacrifice and perceived risk in advance, since resistance is usually traceable to the sacrifice they know is coming and anticipating it is what equips the presenter to manage the apprehension.

Read resistance as protection rather than obstruction: most people resist because the request demands a risk or sacrifice, and what the presenter sees as resistance the audience may experience as valor in defending their reputation, credibility or honour — so acknowledge it as legitimate while assuring them they are in good hands.

Expect emotional turmoil from everyone affected by the change, including those who appear to accept it, because even positive or rational changes involve loss and uncertainty and reactions range from passive resistance through active undermining to sincere embrace.

Do not read intellectual agreement as adoption: an audience can understand and even mentally accept a plea and still not be moved to act, and they push back partly because otherwise they must live with the contradiction between their old position and the new one.

Analyse the refusal of the call along six axes — comfort zone and change tolerance, fears separating the valid from the dispellable, vulnerabilities and recent errors, likely misunderstandings, mental and practical obstacles, and politics or shifts in the balance of power.

Describe a reward that makes the action worthwhile and make the payoff obvious, because no matter how stimulating the plea an audience will not act without one; draw it from the seven categories of basic needs, security, savings, prize, recognition, relationship and destiny, and keep it proportional to the sacrifice being asked.
State the benefit at three widening scopes — what the audience gains personally, what it gives their sphere of influence, and what it does for humanity or the planet.

Recruit external research to support a counter-intuitive ask, as the finding that firms sustaining customer focus and pipeline investment through a downturn can stay ahead for up to five years after recovery was used to justify not cutting marketing.

Do not open presentation software during idea generation; collect and create content first, keep generating along a theme until possibilities are exhausted, and expect the genuinely clever ideas to appear in the third or fourth round rather than the first.

Run idea collection and idea creation as distinct processes — mining existing material wide and deep across studies, competitor insight, news, partner programs and tangential topics, then inventing from instinct — and mine competitors' messages specifically in order to position differently rather than reusing a peer's slides.

Put one idea on each slide and sketch each one small on paper before opening the software, since slides are free, the audience visually re-engages at every advance, and the constrained sketch space forces simple clear words and pictures — with large type beating dense prose where no image exists.

Build the presentation collaboratively even though one person appears on stage: develop a written framework through argument and discussion, then a visual framework of sketches and storyboards, so the ideas are written and drawn before they are performed.

Brainstorm the context — setting, audience, the messages they need, the call to action — before the storyline, and keep the meta-structure visible while resisting the urge to perfect any single idea early.
Generate ideas away from the presentation software with pen and paper in a changed environment, because the application is a container for ideas and assets rather than a means of generating them.

Make quantity the objective of ideation: generate many ideas in any form — words, diagrams, scenes, literal or metaphorical — and keep going even when they wander, rather than stopping at the first idea, because stronger solutions typically surface only after four or five have percolated.
Use emotion to mark which facts matter, because reciting fact after fact never signals importance and forces the audience to work out the decision themselves.
A flat factual register is adequate for a written scientific report but fails for the oral delivery of persuasive content.

Locate content on the head-heart-gut-groin spectrum and correct in whichever direction the presenter defaults: analytical communicators must move lower because many decisions are emotional, while purely emotional communicators lose analytical audiences for lack of proof and damage their own credibility.

Inventory the deck against the analytical and emotional content types and convert wherever appropriate, since a neutral diagram becomes charged once the struggle behind it is told and data stays purely analytical until the presenter explains why the movement happened.

For an audience in a stereotypically analytical profession keep the emotional share small but non-zero, at minimum opening and closing with why, since the reason people entered such a field usually has an emotional component.

Calibrate to the audience's tolerance in both directions: analytical audiences read heavy heartstring-tugging as manipulation yet are still motivated by showing how lives will be changed, while emotionally driven audiences want to know the details were considered but need only a few proof points rather than twenty slides of them.
Practise integrative thinking by generating from the emotional regions first — bolder, riskier and more interesting — then deliberately returning to the head to analyse what was produced.
In a cerebral setting a thin veneer of emotional appeal goes a long way: adding why the work matters alongside how it works makes a technical case inspirational as well as instructive.
Take a strong and clear position, because that is what opens space for a compelling counter-position, and move back and forth between the poles to keep the audience engaged.

Recognize that the what-is versus what-could-be gap need not be today against tomorrow: it can be the customer without the product against with it, or the world from an alternate point of view against the presenter's — the gap is any contrast between where the audience is and where they could be.

Pair every brainstormed point with its intelligent counterargument during preparation even if the counterargument is never delivered, since confronting the audience's alternate perspective earns credibility — and an analysis of 476 British political speeches found half of all applause bursts followed a moment of contrast.
Contrasting the commonplace with the lofty is what produces the up-and-down shapeliness of the presentation form.

Attach a human to every feature, because specifications are meaningless until an attribute visibly affects a person — that is where meaning resides — and sharing the experience as a story creates a shared experience and visceral connection.

Answer why before what and how: a technical description can be accurate and succinct yet fail because it ignores why anyone should care, and the reason to care starts with a story supplying a human element.
Hook the audience with the story before revealing the mechanism, because explaining how a magic trick works before performing it loses them.

Build the embedded story to a known shape: introduce the hero early with a reason to root for them, set up the conflict without revealing how it is overcome, reveal a solution that is not easy, raise the stakes with a secondary challenge, then resolve incrementally so the final movement lifts the hero from one state to another.
Place the technical or data-heavy explanation at a story cliffhanger, which keeps the audience in suspense, privileges them with information the characters lack, and still delivers the hard data.

Give numbers a narrative because they rarely speak for themselves: explain scale by contrast with familiar-size items, compare against similar-value figures from another context, and supply the environmental and strategic context behind the movement — leaving bumps, anomalies and trends to individual interpretation forfeits the meaning.
Run divergent and convergent thinking repeatedly rather than once each, and use the big idea itself as the filter — eliminating every piece of collected material that does not distinctly support it.
After filtering, re-check that enough interesting contrast survived, because contrast must not be lost on the cutting-room floor during vetting.

Cluster surviving content into roughly three to five major topics with three to five supporting ideas each, and test the set with MECE — mutually exclusive so topics do not overlap and confuse, collectively exhaustive so nothing the audience expects is conspicuously missing.

Convert every topic into a full, emotionally charged sentence before structuring, because topics are neutral and messages are charged — and give each message as much contrast as its point needs, such as acknowledging a prior failure before announcing its successor.
Assume the presentation has too many ideas rather than too few: exploring hundreds is correct, but only the most potent may be conveyed.

Structure outside the slide application: linear tools push attention onto individual slides, so lay the content out spatially on sticky notes, a wall or the floor to expose holes, keep the whole in view, and see how much weight and time each portion is receiving.

Build the structure around the audience's comprehension rather than the expert's mental map, since subject-matter experts naturally link ideas adjacent in their own minds and those relationships are invisible to the audience.
Give the audience a stake in the idea through strong visual grammar that engages more than one sense, because that is how an idea gets adopted as their own rather than merely heard.

Review with an outline rather than a slide show, and review structure holistically, so reviewers absorb the whole at once, find their own concerns immediately, and give faster, more thoughtful feedback while the presenter stays focused on the construct rather than the details.

Choose the organizational pattern deliberately from four storylike structures — chronological, sequential, spatial and climactic — and four with contrast built in that suit persuasion — problem-solution, compare-contrast, cause-effect and advantage-disadvantage — using them either as the overarching structure or within a subtopic.
Characterize the organization with verbs describing what it does rather than adjectives describing what it is, and let those verbs drive the visual choices.

Treat message order as a lever on outcome, since placing one piece of information beside another creates meaning; the same material resequenced so each point builds on the last, with a little emotional appeal added, turns a demotivating update into a motivating crescendo.
Orchestrate the audience's communal physical response — laughter, gasps, applause — as an integral part of the telling rather than an accident of it.
Check that emotion shifts across the talk the way screenwriters check beats within a scene, moving between pain and pleasure so the audience stays engaged.

Plant one S.T.A.R. moment — Something They'll Always Remember — significant, sincere and enlightening enough to become watercooler talk or a headline, chosen from memorable dramatization, repeatable sound bites, evocative visuals, emotive storytelling or shocking statistics, and built to magnify the big idea rather than distract from it.
Weight the S.T.A.R. moment most heavily when the audience is comparing several presenters and will decide weeks later, since the presenter needs to be the one still remembered.
Meter the amount of new information delivered before each climax, since that pacing is what lets a presenter grab attention and carry it forward.
Memorable moments are repeated and retransmitted so they travel further than the presentation itself, and audience interest is directly proportionate to the presenter's preparation.
Keep the S.T.A.R. moment free of kitsch and matched to the specific audience — an overly emotionally charged device is wrong for a technical audience — or it reads as a bad camp skit.

Prefer a physical demonstration that settles the point in seconds over an argument about it, and consider introducing the prop early and leaving it unexplained so suspense builds until the moment it pays off.

Craft memorable phrases in advance rather than trusting the moment — historically quoted lines were mindfully planned — and make a crafted phrase stick by repeating it more than once, punctuating it with a pause long enough for the audience to write it down, and projecting the words so it lands visually as well as orally.
Build sound bites with named rhetorical devices — imitating a famous phrase, or repeating words at the beginning, middle or end of a series.

Use images where words cannot carry the emotional force, because recalling an image also recalls the emotion attached to it, and pair images deliberately to create conflicted emotion or jarring contrast — an advantage that is strongest for abstract issues.

Weave one master story through the whole talk against a master theme, referring back to it repeatedly, and close by returning to the premise of the opening story so the audience arrives where they started with new insight.

When neutrally presented data has repeatedly failed to produce action, change the format rather than the facts: the identical information retold visually with emotional urgency moved citizens and officials that seven years of reports had not.
Repeat one deliberate phrase several times in the talk while using identical wording in the press release, which is what drives the press to adopt it as the headline.
Recast a shocking statistic at a scale the audience can feel rather than stating the raw number.

Work with the audience's snap judgment rather than against it: Aristotle held trust should come from the speech itself, but today's audiences do judge in the first seconds, and the impression is made not by gimmicks but by revealing character, motivations, abilities and vulnerabilities.

Where special terminology is genuinely required, be prepared to translate it into lay language, know when to switch registers, and choose only words inside the listener's vocabulary — tailoring the language to what the audience actually uses.

Communication style can bury a genuine discovery for decades, as with a 1940s genetics finding that went misunderstood until the 1970s because the presenter's rapid leaps from observation to model to conclusion outpaced her audiences.

Brevity does not require dropping the form: a 278-word, two-minute address outlasted a two-hour eulogy on the same platform while still stating what is, showing what could be, issuing a call to action, and closing on the new bliss.
Keep any single slide on screen for no more than two minutes, since film analysts hold scenes under three minutes and the presentation medium is more static than cinema.

Run the screening properly: give each screener a printout of slides and notes, run the whole presentation once and then revisit each section, and budget roughly three times the presentation's length for the review.
Use deliberate constraint on yourself and your media as the mechanism for breaking dependence on slides, expecting it to take real work and commitment.
Verify the content is readable at every screen size on which it will be consumed, and change the visual aid to suit the audience rather than assuming slides are the only option.
Accept that one idea per slide produces more slides than a traditional deck; that is acceptable rather than a fault.
Reorganize a weak deck conceptually rather than cosmetically: thinking outside the existing slides can reveal that the underlying structure differs from what the old deck asserted.

Separate the document from the presentation: a request for material that will be read on its own is a request for a document, which should be as comprehensive as it needs to be, while sparse slides are for presenting.
Apply kairos — speaking in the right moment in the right way — by understanding the situation, cross-checking it, and modifying the presentation's emotional and analytical balance to fit.

Treat the rhetorical triangle as dynamic rather than an equal balance: a broad audience responds viscerally, is receptive to emotion and needs a story-weighted structure, while an analytical audience responds cerebrally, is suspicious of emotion and needs a report-weighted structure.
Host a screening before delivery to filter out meandering structure, obstructed messages and confusing language, arriving expecting to rework a share of the material.

A presentation's quality will not exceed the quality of the planning process that precedes it, following Conway's Law that a design mirrors the communication structure of the organization that produced it.
If a business is a decision factory, the presentations that inform its decisions determine those decisions' quality.

Staff the screening with people matching the target audience profile and include deliberate naysayers who will scrutinize, criticize and challenge, going outside the organization for honest feedback whenever the internal review culture is sugar-sweet or dysfunctional.
Acting on rehearsal feedback requires a humble stance, because it means adding material while cutting pieces the presenter has grown fond of.

Treat rehearsal as the missing discipline rather than an optional finish, because actors are effective through hours of memorization and delivery practice while the visual triggers a presenter leaves on slides mean nothing to the audience.

Teach a complex subject by pitching explanations, analogies and metaphors at the audience's level using items already familiar to them, isolating the whole into layers, explaining and demonstrating each separately, and only then presenting the complete thing so its nuances become perceptible — vetting each metaphor for that specific audience.

Close the improvement loop after every delivery: review the recording, identify specific fixes so the same mistakes are not repeated, and treat practice as never reaching perfection — rehearse, re-rehearse, solicit feedback, review, refine again.

An idea confined to one mind is not alive; it becomes alive as it is adopted person by person toward a tipping point, so frame the vision such that every listener holds a share of responsibility for it.

Plan for many deliveries rather than one, because systemic adoption takes repeated presentation of the same idea over years, and treat each communication milestone as a catalyst in its own right — an opportunity to adjust strategy, collaborate and realign, where the discussions held in preparation sometimes carry as much value as the presentation.

A warning buried in a dense deck and softened by conciliatory notes does not function as a warning; when the presentation's purpose is to alert decision-makers to a risk, state it plainly and unmissably.

The communicator's job is to make others see the idea, because ideas gain traction on being seen — and getting stakeholders to understand while a competitor's concepts stay obscure is itself the competitive advantage, since a clearly presented smart idea becomes the spark that mobilizes resources.
Imagining a future in which the idea has been implemented is what keeps a communicator able to argue for it passionately.

All the smarts in the world are useless if they are not understood: a firm the client judged smarter lost a multimillion-dollar bid because dense, smart-sounding slides obscured its findings while the rival communicated usably.
Match the contour's pace to the occasion's energy — a rapid oscillation between what is and what could be suits a gathering of heightened collective energy rather than serving as a universal tempo.

Use dramatic pauses, repeated word sequences and a recurring refrain, and build images in the mind with metaphor and visual language, varying pace to produce distinct crescendos that build toward the closing description of the new bliss.

Establish common ground by quoting material the audience already holds — familiar songs, scripture, literature and the founding documents of their institution — so the argument lands on ground they already accept.
There is always one person in the audience to whom the communicator is really speaking, so the work is justified even when it visibly reaches only that one.
Embody the emotion rather than describing it, and accept that some feelings cannot be put into words so the material may legitimately aim to be felt rather than understood.

Produce original material by sustained accumulation rather than waiting for inspiration: record thoughts, observations, impressions and quotations over time, read widely across unrelated fields, and write out a detailed script once the notes reveal a pattern.
Fear of presenting is surmountable by repeated attempts rather than by talent, as demonstrated by a performer who once fled the room in panic and went on to lecture for decades.
Amid a great deal of disingenuous noise, an idea presented with sincerity and passion is what stands out and resonates.

Exploit the sonata's lesson that structure lets listeners anticipate what comes next: introduce and repeat the theme so the audience thoroughly grasps it, alter it to create tension and surprise, then restate it — since the initial grasp is precisely what makes the later gap between what is and what could be identifiable.
Layer several kinds of contrast at once — as music layers tonal, dynamic and textural contrast — because contrast across varying layers is what keeps the whole interesting.
Follow the form while working flexibly inside it, as sonatas obey standard rules yet never sound contrived because great composers flex within the constraint.

Envision the presentation in enough detail beforehand that the script becomes unnecessary during delivery, and honour the collaborators by using their strengths and staying open to modifying the vision they expand upon.

Choose the execution that best serves the idea — a multi-slide scene, a manipulated image, a custom illustration, a short video — rather than the cheapest to execute, and bring in a designer when the chosen concept exceeds the presenter's own skill.
Know the rules before breaking them, because rule-breaking grounded in full command of the form creates meaning while rule-breaking without it creates noise.

Expect an idea far outside convention to be rejected first and persist anyway, since persistence moves an idea from rejected to considered to adopted, and standing out enough to be noticed can carry the cost of being reviled.
Use the big idea to filter out every frequency other than the resonant one, and treat structure as greater than the sum of its parts.

Attribute the method's borrowed foundations rather than treating them as original: the noise-in-communication model is Shannon's, retrofitted to presentations, and the claim that an audience cannot listen and read simultaneously rests on Mayer's multimedia-learning research while the contrast-and-applause finding rests on Heritage and Greatbatch's 1986 study.
Distinguish illustration from evidence in this material: the book itself flags its NASA janitor anecdote as an urban legend of sorts, so such stories demonstrate a point rather than establish it.

Treat this method's advice as conditional rather than universal, as the source explicitly disclaims that its strategies suit every situation and directs the reader to a professional where appropriate.
Presentation literacy functions as competitive advantage whether the goal is closing a deal, advancing a cause, or engaging staff.
Be intentional: tell the story on purpose and set out deliberately to cause the change being claimed, and judge success by the audience's transformation rather than by the delivery of the deck.
Treat a customer-facing presentation as a brand touchpoint and hold it to the standard applied to paid marketing, because it is often the last impression before a purchase decision.
Give message, visual story, and delivery comparable attention; a deck that only develops the message leg is incomplete.

Derive the deck's visual system from the story's own setting rather than an industry default, using materials, textures, and framing that put the audience inside the world of the message — and use a subtle gradient behind a chart where contrast needs help.
Reject visual dissonance — mismatched perspective, inconsistent light sources, jarring animation — because it leaves the audience agitated, less receptive, and can cost the presenter trust.
Re-cut the content whenever the delivery channel changes; material built for in-person delivery does not transfer unmodified to a web or mass-media audience.
Plan for iteration rather than a single pass: exploration, informal input, and review cycles are what produce the stronger result.

Answer the seven audience questions and build one persona per distinct audience segment before any slide is built, keeping the persona slide at the front of the deck as private working context that is never projected.
Express invisible ideas as stories with fitting imagery, because stories are how people understand and relate to the world.
Close ideation with an explicit filter: classify, challenge, and reduce the volume of ideas to a small core set that meets the objective being communicated.

Use a one-idea-per-sticky-note discipline written with a broad marker, and treat an idea that outgrows the note or the marker as too complex; the point is fast, re-orderable capture, so linear storyboarding is an equally valid method.
Treat simplicity as the essence of clear communication and let the slide's form embody its message — a message of simplicity must be carried by slides that feel simple.
Let type alone carry a message where it can: often a single word or phrase is all a slide needs.

Treat sketching as an iterative loop — rough, refine, re-organize, re-sketch until a story is visible — and disregard drawing quality, since the first sketch is the most obvious one and further passes yield better ideas.

Use the sketch stage as proof-of-concept and expect to throw nearly everything away: ideas that are too complex, slow, or costly surface there, and discarding all but one is the intended destructive half of the creative process.
Produce a hand-drawn overlay by tracing over a printed photo, scanning the sketch, making its background transparent, and layering — and animate it where that adds meaning.
Draw figures body-first — body, then head placed relative to it, then face, then legs, then arms — because the body and legs carry the gesture that communicates the idea.

Test-drive sketches on a colleague before going live: ask whether the sketches capture the intent independently of the spoken words, and have them ask clarifying questions or draw their own version when confused.

For a cross-cultural audience, carry the message in culturally neutral images rather than bullets, keep graphics extremely simple because not all cultures read left to right, and animate the reveal to guide processing order.
Keep sketching loose and fast against reference imagery, and compose inside the actual slide format so spatial fit is proven before any digital build.
Communicate the intended look with reference images that convey the feel of the final artwork when the sketches alone do not carry the vision to collaborators.

Brief an illustrator with the story to be told rather than with what to draw, give them time for research, ideation, and revision — or a sketch when time is short and the vision is clear — trust their expertise over untrained subjective opinion, and consolidate all stakeholder feedback into one non-conflicting direction.
