Reach for a diagram when the point is how the parts of a whole interact, and pick its type deliberately from the taxonomy of abstract forms (flow, structure, cluster, radiate) and realistic forms (pictorial, displayed data) rather than defaulting to a familiar shape.
Select the pictorial diagram from its communicative job — process, reveal, direction, location, or influence — so the illustration answers the question the audience actually has.

Select the flow diagram from the shape of the process itself: linear for a definite start and end, circular for a process with no end point, divergent or convergent when elements split or collide, and multidirectional for complex combined relationships.

Select the structure diagram from what is being structured: a matrix to compare two or more data sets, a tree for clear hierarchy, and layers for elements that stack and so carry both hierarchy and sequence.

Select the cluster diagram from the relationship being asserted — overlapping for shared responsibility, closure for a whole greater than its parts, enclosure to mark a higher order, and a linking element to group related items.

Select the radiate diagram from the origin structure: from a point for a burst with a clear origin, with a core for a parent-child relationship, and without a core when elements cohere only by proximity.

Spend the extra thinking time to unify a diagram set around a central character or motif, which gives the individual concepts context, sequence, and association instead of leaving them merely adequate.

Present data with absolute integrity: be ready to supply the complete data set on request and to defend the conclusions, and avoid ornamenting data because decoration costs credibility — especially with analytically trained audiences who read over-simplified data as manipulated marketing material.
Drop the chart entirely when the slide carries a single key message or a single number, since removing it can increase the slide's impact.
Hold chart geometry constant across consecutive chart slides so axes do not jump between slides.

Choose between pie and bar by what the audience must read: a pie only for large proportional differences — first set at twelve o'clock, at most eight sections, totalling 100 percent — and a bar whenever precise relationships or larger or stacked data sets are involved.

Strip chartjunk from data slides — surplus lines, ticks, gradients, borders, fills, and 3D depth that skews the data — because simplicity matters more here than anywhere else, since the data can already confuse the viewer.

Audit chart colour for unintended meaning and for focal clarity: red conventionally marks negative values so a red brand colour belongs on non-data elements, an entity must keep one colour across paired charts, tilted pies distort foreground weight, and too many bold colours destroy the focal point — reproportion the chart instead.

When the goal is to move people emotionally to act, use raw, real photographs found by digging through many candidates, because staged stock imagery lacks the credibility and import that real photos carry.

Select photography as a family that reads as one photographer's work with consistent lighting and colour tone, favouring realism over staged or metaphorical stock situations that do not occur in real life.
Shoot a custom photograph when no stock image tells the story: decide what picture is needed before searching, light the subjects carefully, and let planning remove the need for later digital repair.

Replace bare numbers with icons that let the audience see the statistic, and isolate each statistic as a large statement on its own slide rather than competing on a crowded one, since bullets are only one option for displaying text.
Attribute presentation improvement to internalizing the subject, rehearsing the delivery, and taking expert guidance, because a presentation built that way can tap emotion and shift mass perception.
Expect clutter removal to take courage, practice, and trial and error, and accept more nervous energy at first as the presentation shifts toward connection with the audience.
Respect the limit on how much new information a person can process and remove non-essential visual material, since supporting visuals that add load work against understanding.

Use arrangement as the primary lever on clarity, and pick the tool by the audience outcome required: contrast to find the main point, flow to fix processing order, hierarchy to show relationships, unity to signal belonging, proximity to convey meaning from location, and whitespace to give breathing room.

Define design as making communication as easy and clear for the viewer as possible rather than as decoration: instead of prettier talking points, display information so that complex information becomes clear.
Apply contrast by the smallest effective difference: use just-noticeable, definitive, minimal differences, remembering that larger text reads as most important wherever it sits.
Base every stylistic choice on a defined purpose, because any difference between two elements signals importance, urgency, or value, and unintentional contrast confuses or contradicts the message.
Design for the conditioned Z-shaped reading path — top left, back and forth, then meaning assigned — as the default the audience brings to every slide.
Point the composition at the content: images of people should look toward the content rather than away from it, and a data chart's reading direction must be obvious at a glance.

Bound each slide's information load concretely: at most three layers on a plane, one main point with no more than two sub-points, deliberate internal flow, and images or diagrams whose direction leads to the focal point or the next slide.

Make the visual hierarchy mirror the information hierarchy exactly, since hierarchy is processed almost as fast as contrast and a bullet heavier than its own title breaks the logic the audience is reading.
Set relative size and proximity deliberately, because changing them changes the story the diagram tells about which element dominates.
State the intended message explicitly and verify the graphical hierarchy carries it, because an audience left to interpret will construct its own meaning.

Achieve unity through structure, look, and theme, and use a grid of rectangular regions as the structural layer so elements are anchored, placement patterns become predictable, and equivalent elements such as chart axes stop jumping between consecutive slides.
Vary element shapes and sizes within a regular grid to produce structure and solidity, and leave the top and bottom channels empty for a cinematic frame that also reserves title space.
Fix content positions across the template so the audience learns where to look and content never bounces between slides, varying placement only where a design purpose requires it.
Adopt a grid at organizational scale to streamline independent authors' design decisions and make slides reusable across decks.

Install a template system as soon as more than one person builds presentations, because it raises productivity, constrains exploration, protects the brand investment, and lowers the design skill each author needs.
Use a web-based presentation application when authors in different locations must build one deck simultaneously, with the result viewable online or downloaded for offline delivery.

Build the grid as a working tool: sketch it, place elements into it while deliberately leaving tiles open as clear space, put the guides on the master slide, remove them before delivery, and save the grid for reuse.
Break the grid only as an exception to focus attention, because repeated grid-breaking destroys the effect.

Place associated elements intentionally to preempt unintended readings, because relative placement tells a secondary story — antagonism or protagonism, chaos or order, decline or growth — and human subjects carry conventional meanings by edge, height, isolation, opposition, and surrounding space.

Fix element styles and hold them consistent so they become visual triggers of the brand, and spend a deliberate inconsistency only once, since breaking the rules routinely forfeits the emphasis entirely.

Design the background as a deliberate surface — opacity, texture, and light source chosen on purpose, default templates and their ornamentation abandoned — that serves the information instead of competing with it, keeping it open, spacious, and clean because ornamented templates can consume a third of the usable area.

Derive the background from the timeless visual elements already present in the organization's marketing material — grid, line structures, bounding boxes, palette — rather than from application defaults.

Commit the whole deck to either a 2D or a 3D space and never mix them: flat bold colour minimizes complexity, while a single glisten or shadow commits every element to a three-dimensional environment.

Once in a 3D space, enforce the laws of environmental consistency file-wide — one vanishing point, one light source, one consistent effect on elements — because elements that do not map to the established environment leave the audience unsettled and subliminally frustrated.
Choose the slide's environment consciously, since one is established the moment a graphic is drawn whether or not the presenter intended it.

Treat every movement as an involuntary attention magnet: humans are hard-wired to look at what moves, so unpurposed animation inevitably pulls attention off the presenter, every change costs some grasp of the content, and animation is justified only where it helps the audience process information.
Choose live projection when the goal is shared energy the other media cannot translate, and accept that the screen will visually dominate the presenter in that setting.

Construct a consistent 3D scene from a horizon on a grid-of-thirds line and a single vanishing point, matching every object's angles to it rather than mixing angles — or use an isometric grid, which has neither.
Choose the light source first when depth is used, because it determines how light and shadow fall on both the background and every object placed on it.

Work from the colour wheel that the presentation applications' pickers implement, and pick a scheme for the contrast and tension it produces — monochromatic needing black, white, and greys; analogous for a narrow warm or cool harmony; complementary limited to two for maximum contrast; split complementary for contrast with less tension; triadic for vivid interest; tetradic for strong contrast needing one dominant colour.

Assemble a palette of three to five core colours plus a neutral and a highlight, starting from logo or industry colours — and derive an industry palette by sampling from images that support the subject matter, choosing which part of those images to draw from.

Assign each palette role a job: neutrals for background surfaces, hierarchy, divisions of space, and secondary data so emphasized data stands out; highlights only for accentuating text and emphasis in charts; and explicit light and dark tones to define gradient range.

Design for colour vision deficiency in about one viewer in twelve by varying brightness and shape rather than hue alone, and test by converting the deck to greyscale and printing it in black and white — whatever disappears there may disappear for those viewers.
Search for images with the palette open so they fit it, and dress models in complementary wardrobe when shooting original photography.

Choose a typeface by studying its anatomy — height, weight, ascenders and descenders, counters, x-height — so it reflects the intended personality, and use true typographic apostrophes rather than foot marks.

Match serif and sans serif to the job — serifs for multi-line running copy where the feet hold the eye on the line, sans serif for short bursts such as headlines and captions — while treating the claim that slides must be sans serif as unsettled, since the legibility studies are inconclusive.

Limit a presentation to two typefaces, one for headlines and subheads and one for body copy, with a single typeface being perfectly acceptable and emphasis achieved through colour or italics rather than a third font.
Keep titles to one line because of the eye distance a second line adds, and consider a titles-only deck.
Animate text only when the motion adds value, meaning, or emotion to the content.
Apply typographic craft to display text — ligatures where letterforms join, auto-kerning on with manual kerning of A, R, T, V, W, and Y, and tracking adjusted for word density.

Set blocks of text with the distinction between paragraph and line spacing in hand — each bullet is a paragraph, a wrapped line is not — space sub-bullets so each associates with its own parent, and check the rag for distracting shape and widows, fixing them by text-block width or manual soft returns.

Write bullets as newspaper headlines the presenter will flesh out: succinct, in parallel structure with the same tense, part of speech, and sentence-or-fragment form, and without sub-bullets wherever possible.

Apply one capitalization and punctuation convention across the whole deck — conventionally title case for titles and initial caps elsewhere, or the organization's own guidelines — reserving all caps for sparing emphasis because caps read as shouting.

Fill dead screen time at large venues with a walk-in animation of quotes, imagery, or video matched to the event theme, reusing the same assets as interstitials during breaks and demo switches, because such animations are cheap to produce yet carry real impact.
Fill an idle screen with calm ambient imagery so the audience stays with the message rather than looking at a dead display.
Maintain a shared library of reusable, pre-approved image parts so key design decisions are already made and authors spend their effort on content rather than on hunting for assets.

Vet images of people against explicit criteria: reflecting the audience's culture or ethnicity, context-appropriate, not cropped at the neck, representing real industry and customer situations, and current to the era.

Compose photographs on a grid of thirds with key features at the power points, because an off-centre focal point reads as balanced and energetic, holds more interest than a centred subject, and leaves open space for slide text.

Choose illustration lines for their temperament — straight and sharp reads analytical, curved reads casual — assign line styles to distinct purposes as a system, and stay consistent, remembering that the thinnest lines may not project at all in a large venue and that textured lines require tools outside the presentation software.

Build an industry-relevant icon library, bought or commissioned, and draw it in isometric style with no vanishing point so every icon sits on the same implied surface and can be arranged and connected freely.
Consider giving an art library away to the entire industry, competitors included, when pioneering a category, so your representations become the standard.
Build and animate a complex infographic over time so the audience grasps how the parts interconnect, and bring in a professional illustrator once the illustration exceeds in-house skill.

Standardize illustration and diagram style on one texture, light source, and pattern unless the concept genuinely demands more, never use clip art, and when buying illustrations choose ones that read as a single illustrator's work.
Use short video slides of a few seconds to half a minute where a complex point is best carried by motion, judging them on the creativity of the idea rather than on production polish.
Design the time-based layer deliberately as a communication strategy rather than adding animation at the end, identifying in advance the specific places where motion earns its cost.
Pick animation pace for the intended feeling — slow pans for nostalgia or the passage of time, quick cuts for excitement, energy, or surprise.
Justify each animation against the five legitimate purposes — change in relationship, direction, change in object, sequence, and emphasis — and discard motion that serves none of them.

Plan pacing, travel path, and object position because they determine both processing speed and how far the audience's eyes must move; reject gratuitous motion such as text bouncing into place, and combine several effects where one cannot render the story naturally.

Audit animation against the failure list: unnatural or counterintuitive movement, frenetic or chronic pace, no value or purpose, distraction from the presenter, use just because the feature exists, so many animations that the purpose blurs, a style inappropriate to the content, or a sudden motion that startles.

Exploit the built-in meaning of screen direction: left-to-right reads easy because it mimics reading, downward motion reads natural under gravity, and the right-to-left ascent is the hardest direction of all because it fights both reading and gravity.
Give distant entrances and exits a path-based animation plus scaling against an established horizon and vanishing point, so objects grow and shrink between background and foreground.

Treat animation as capable of costing audience outright — overzealous motion has induced motion sickness in a tenth of a room — so the presence of a feature is no reason to use it and specific animations should be banned where they conflict with the brand.

Centralize design decisions with a few individuals and publish the reasoning behind them in written guidelines, because employees are brand ambassadors who express the brand daily and authors who understand the logic apply it consistently and accurately.

Build the template from the brand's timeless visual attributes rather than from a current campaign, using only the elements an audit shows to be essential rather than decorative, because re-creating a template across a large company tanks productivity.
Keep the template a basic shell for words and images rather than a stand-alone work of art.
Decide the template-versus-slide boundary empirically by collecting and auditing real files from many departments to find the actual communication patterns.

Consult IT before building a template: check the application's upgrade path so the template targets the release in use, and confirm storage, because image-heavy decks multiply into terabytes within a department.
Ship both a light and a dark variant of the template so the identity survives large formal projection and ad-hoc printing alike.
Design the branded walk-in and transition screens first, exploring several options rather than the first obvious one, and then use the chosen look as the building block for every other layout.

Scope template guidelines to the organization's actual communication needs — diagram pages, chart types, image-usage layouts, or Gantt charts and roadmaps as appropriate — showing the chosen design decision for each content form and providing multiples of a layout where needed.

Cover the full layout inventory in a template: segue slides for walk-in, title, transition, and Q&A walk-out; content slides for text, text with graphic, quote, and charts and tables; and the components — grid, palette, component style, and image overview.
Hold the slide to its intended role: a mnemonic visual aid that helps the audience retain and recall — the stage and costume providing context, never the star of the show.
Never read the slide text aloud, because the audience detects it immediately and reads ahead, leaving presenter and audience out of sync.

Wean the deck off text with the reduce-record-repeat routine: rehearse, highlight one keyword per bullet, rehearse from the keyword alone, then delete everything else and prefer an image; record the delivery and listen back; and repeat the content aloud and from memory using flash cards, mind maps, or a summary before the final cut.
Account for the screen dwarfing the presenter — around eight times a person in a business venue and nearly forty in a large keynote — because that dominance pulls focus away from the speaker.

For a consensus-seeking pitch, use the ten-slide, twenty-minute, thirty-point-minimum discipline and cover the ten investor topics — problem, solution, business model, underlying technology, marketing and sales, competition, team, projections and milestones, status and timeline, and a summary with call to action — planning twenty minutes of an hour slot because setup and attendance losses consume the rest.

Do not apply a slide-count rule as one-size-fits-all: when the audience needs written detail to study and circulate, put the script and supporting text in the notes area and design the notes master so the printed handout carries all the content at near-brochure quality.

Rebuild the deck as a self-contained brochure when it will be consumed online without a presenter: complete thoughts and phrases across slides with simple images, because there is no narration to supply the missing half — and the reach earns the investment, since one deck can be seen by millions.
Use web upload and collaborative building as a cheap distribution and conferencing channel that lets others embed the deck.

Re-author for each distribution format rather than reusing one deck: handheld delivery needs accompanying audio and slides built for the scale since 24-point type can reduce to an unreadable 4 points, web video must stay inside the roughly ten-minute site limits, and a web cast tolerates more text but needs bite-size bursts where distraction is high.
Use a real, tangible prop — a rare object, a costume, a revealed surprise — to drive a point home, provided it still reads from the stage or under video magnification.

Deliver as a person rather than an automaton, because the presenter's own experience and passion are what set the talk apart while the format pushes toward metronomic delivery with the presenter's back to the audience and the applications do not help.
Engineer moments of clarity — appealing to visual as well as verbal senses and guiding comprehension rather than hindering it — because that is where epiphanies and moving experiences come from.
